Person Work Deliverable this round --- --- --- A: Owner Confirm requirements, invite members, adjust assignments, request revisions, adopt, and close out Two adoption records and a project summary B: Member Compute excerpt total counts for 7 samples and subset CPM for 50 genes Two README versions, plus a separate member-qc-notes.md member note C: Member Read B's adopted version 2 and compare treated / untreated group means One descriptive comparison README To follow along, first prepare the count data and sample annotation from the public source, then provide the inputs to the project. 1. A writes the requirements and confirms two serial modules A writes the real excerpt, output scope, and dependencies on the requirements page: B first produces the QC and subset CPM report; C uses only B's adopted version. Once it is complete, A checks the modules and confirms the requirements. You can adapt the following target wording and fill in the actual data and sample annotation in the input area: text Module 1: Using the attached 50-gene × 7-sample counts, report each sample's excerpt total count, subset CPM, zero-count proportion, and column-sum check. The README includes the methods, reproducible code, and limitations. Members may attach their own check notes, which the owner previews and reviews. Module 2: Depends on module 1's adopted result; read its report and the member note, and compare the mean subset CPM of the treated and untreated groups, listing the 5 genes with the largest absolute mean difference. Descriptive comparison only; do not report p-values, FDR, or significance conclusions. Figure 1: The inputs, output scope, and dependencies are written into the task description for members to read before accepting. What to check : C's module depends on B's adopted results; "B's AI has finished" is not a start condition for downstream work. 2. A invites members and assigns module 1 to B After confirming the requirements, A invites B and C and checks the task assignments. The system's initial assignment differs from the target division of work, so A reassigns module 1 to B through the UI; B reads the task and accepts. Figure 2: Module 1's member is B; module 2 stays in the inbox, waiting for module 1 to be adopted. What to check : go by the member and status on the task card, not by natural-language descriptions of the division of work. 3. B reviews the draft and submits two files After the local AI generates the README, B previews the report, adds member-qc-notes.md through Add material → Upload from this computer , and edits the result note. The version 1 manifest contains two items: the AI README and the member note. Figure 3: The member reviews and then submits; the attached note is kept as a separate file. Before submitting, B checked the 350 subset CPM values and recorded the calculation method, the verification results, and the items that need owner review in the result note. Tip : before submitting, check both the file content and the result note so that the values, the text, and the work completed this round agree. 4. A requests revisions and B submits version 2 A previews the sealed version 1 and uses Request revision to have B correct the review-status description, keep the separate note, and add per-sample zero-count counts, proportions, and a CPM column-sum check. B revises, reviews again, and submits version 2; A previews this version and adopts it. Version 1 remains in history. Figure 4: The new version is used for this review; the old version can still be expanded. What to check : a revision produces a new delivery version; before adopting, be clear about which version you are previewing. 5. C accepts the downstream task and reads the adopted results Only after B's version 2 is adopted does module 2 become assignable. A reassigns it to C before acceptance; C accepts and runs it. The system places B's version 2 README and member note into C's task inputs, so no manual copying is needed. Figure 5: The project has adopted 1/2, and downstream C is running. Downstream uses B's adopted version 2 files; C can read these inputs directly in their own task and continue the analysis. 6. C previews the report, and A adopts and closes the project C previews the report, confirms that only adopted inputs were used and that the descriptive-analysis limits are kept, then submits. A previews C's sealed report and adopts it; once all modules are complete, A fills in the summary and confirms closeout. Figure 6: The report scopes the data and does not interpret mean differences as statistical significance. Figure 7: Both modules are complete, and the project itself is closed out. Case outcomes Stage Result --- --- Requirement capture and confirmation Two real work modules with dependencies Review and adding material The AI README is sealed together with the member note Revision and version retention B delivered two versions; A adopted version 2 Downstream handoff C used B's adopted version 2 report and member note Human adoption and closeout Both modules adopted; the project is finally complete This case shows the full collaboration flow from requirements to delivery. The analysis uses a data excerpt and a descriptive comparison, so read the results together with the relevant data scope and methods. Further reading - Collaboration guide: button paths, statuses, failure handling, and data boundaries. - Runtime and models: prepare the execution environment and structured output configuration. - Feature status and limitations: what the current version supports.

en.title: Scientific Figures: complex data and reproducibility stress test
en.description: Use multi-file longitudinal measurements, a missing-value matrix, and failure recovery to check a real plotting workflow.
en.body: Scientific Figures: complex data and reproducibility stress test These cases come from actual SciForge operations on 2026-11-05. The data is explicitly constructed synthetic test data , used to expose problems in the software and the analysis workflow; it does not represent real experimental findings. The Python runs, frozen snapshots, logs, images, and documents were all actually saved; the images are not UI mockups. Read the Scientific Figures guide first. This page focuses on checking whether the inputs are explicit, the statistics are correct, the history is retained, and a failure affects the current figure. Case 1: multi-file longitudinal data, cleaning, and a four-panel figure Inputs and rules - Measurement table: 12 samples, 5 time points each, 60 records in total. - Sample table: sample ID, control/treated group, and batch. - Explicit exclusions: 2 null/NA rows and 1 QC fail row, 3 in total; 57 rows retained, with no imputation. - Compute the mean, sample standard deviation (ddof=1), and SEM by group/hour; do not draw error bars when the effective n is less than 2. - Sample IDs must match one-to-one; duplicate or unmatched IDs must raise an explicit error. text Merge the measurement table with the sample information and freeze both source files. After cleaning, save the data and the cleaning rules separately, then include them as inputs to the plotting version. Plot mean±SEM, individual trajectories, a 48-hour scatter, and an effective-n heatmap, and output a QC figure as well. Do not run significance tests; output a complete numeric log and do not auto-accept candidates. Actual results Code complex-longitudinal-v1-20261105 saved the two original CSVs, the cleaned result, and the cleaning-provenance record — 4 input snapshots in total. Run complex-longitudinal-run1-20261105 succeeded and published the first figure to complex-longitudinal-doc-20261105 . This run produced two PNGs. An independent calculation checked n, mean, and SEM item by item for 10 group/hour combinations. For example, control at 12 h has n=5 and mean=12.34; treated at 48 h has n=5, mean=29.86, and SEM≈0.424264. No measurement unit was guessed for the data. What this case checked Multi-file joins, re-freezing cleaned data, differing n caused by missing data, the SEM definition, multiple figure outputs from one run, and the link between a figure and a specific run. Source files, cleaning snapshots, code, and logs are all retained, so later edits do not overwrite the previous step. Case 2: missing values, zero variance, and an expression matrix The input is a synthetic 12-gene × 8-sample matrix plus a separate grouping JSON. The matrix has 1 missing cell; Gene12 is all zeros with zero variance. The requirements: compute a per-row z-score using the sample standard deviation, show missing values in gray without imputation, explicitly exclude Gene12 and retain 11 rows, stably sort by treated−control descriptive mean difference, and produce a two-panel heatmap and effect-size figure. Here "effect size" describes the mean difference only and does not indicate statistical significance or a biological conclusion. The actual run complex-expression-run1-20261105 exited with code 0; the log confirmed 1 missing value, Gene12 excluded, and 11 rows retained. The digest of the two-panel output is 5351702b4bc51ac95032d74cc8c0f73c6e8e3e800873c6ff99cbad58ed871f90 . The mean difference is about 6 for the first 4 genes, about 0.133333 for Gene06 (which has the missing value), and 0 for the rest. Tiny floating-point differences affect the ordering of nominally identical effects; do not read that order as scientific priority. This case also exposed a real UI issue: the create form kept the previous optional image path and carried an unrelated old image into the new case. The old image was explicitly marked supplied/unverified, the run figure became a separate candidate, and nothing claimed it was a reproduction. 0.4.0-mvp.9 now clears the previous files and requirements when you enter the create flow. Case 3: nested source, deliberate failure, and recovery Save analysis/main.py and a sibling analysis/helper.py . The entry point first does a plain import helper , prints BEFORE_FAILURE 42 , then deliberately raises DELIBERATE_COMPLEX_CASE_FAILURE . The actual run complex-failure-run1-20261105 failed; it saved that output and exception, produced 0 output figures, and published no figure. A fixed child version complex-recovery-v2-20261105 was then saved, retaining the 4 inputs frozen by the parent and restoring the successful plotting logic while keeping the nested entry point and the helper import. Run complex-recovery-run2-20261105 succeeded and produced two PNGs whose digests matched case 1. It was published as a candidate only, not accepted; the current figure pointer stayed on the original version. This test drove two fixes, shipped in 0.4.0-mvp.9 : a nested entry point imports sibling modules from its own directory first; and when the same run request is repeated or run history is listed, each image also returns the correct storage base directory. Relative paths and digests in storage are not rewritten. Case 4: multiple image paths and the count limit The actual run complex-output-paths-run1-20261105 produced three PNGs: group A/figure.png , group B/figure.png , and 中文 图.PNG . Files with the same name in two different directories were saved independently; spaces, Chinese characters, and an uppercase extension did not cause any figure to be lost. readRun returned the storage base directory for each output, and the digest and length of each output passed verification. Then only the child version parameters were changed to output 17 figures, and complex-output-limit-run2-20261105 was executed. The run was recorded as failed, with 0 publishable outputs and the count-limit diagnostic retained. Even if Python itself completes, exceeding the limit during collection cannot be passed off as a successful figure. Run and reproduction checks For every run, verify: the digest and length of each input snapshot, the code and parent version, the run status/exit code, the environment manifest, the logs, each PNG's file digest, and whether the figure points to the corresponding successful run. After the source data changes, editing the child code should inherit the parent's frozen inputs by default; updating data requires explicitly creating a new input snapshot. A re-run should create a new run ID so that both the original run and the re-run record are retained. The four cases above originally used v8/v9, when CSVs/JSON had to be saved explicitly. v10 closes this gap with first-class artifact saving for PNG and CSV/TSV/JSON/TXT, so analysis files can be frozen directly as inputs for the next step; older records are not rewritten. Numeric logs are still subject to a length limit, and the environment manifest is not a complete binary environment archive. Case 5: analysis artifact handoff, pagination, and submission recovery An actual v10 run, hardening-root-run-v10-20261105 , saved 7 files directly: figure.png , a 1200-byte cleaned.csv , an 81-byte summary.json , rules.txt , and three environment-rebuild files under _environment . An independent read confirmed that the cleaned table really has 57 data rows, with statistics raw=60, retained=57, excluded=3; every digest and length was verified. The follow-up run hardening-child-run-v10-20261105 froze inputs again from the saved cleaned CSV, kept an independent copy of the data, and plotted without manual copying of temporary files. The parent output and child input paths differ, yet both SHA-256 digests are 3e9a9c0b722f9bae558f9fbbe1796721e3a365519e8ac67d4cc821d8bf20d85b ; the actual log confirms FROZEN_ROWS 57 . The environment file contains the exact versions of 12 installed packages and the steps to rebuild the virtual environment; no installation or network download was performed, and it does not claim to be a hash-pinned dependency lock. The recovery test first actually ran Python to generate JSON, then injected a single write failure when committing run.json in the source scheduling test. The process log and results were saved, and the staging directory remained. Then, in the installed plugin, clicking Complete interrupted record committed the original JSON and logs successfully, and only then cleaned up the staging area. Fault injection is a controlled test, not a random incident or a faked successful process. Pagination in the history list was also actually clicked through: the first page scans at most 20 records, and clicking Load more runs loads the next page. Directories that are reserved but not committed are not disguised as terminal records, so a single page may show fewer than 20; one corrupt record does not block the other pages. Screenshot and verification boundaries The UI screenshots come from the actual app, and the original images come from saved PNG bytes. Automated checks cover file digests, decoded PNG dimensions, DOM visibility, and statistical values. This round did not complete a pixel-level visual review: the host visual service was not ready, so we cannot promise that all text is free of overlap or clipping.

en.title: Virtual cell perturbation prediction benchmark
en.description: Use SciForge to organize the data contract, runs, scoring, failure analysis, and reruns for an external perturbation prediction model.
en.body: Virtual cell perturbation prediction benchmark This case is for researchers who already have a perturbation prediction model and a compute environment. SciForge organizes the data, code, run records, results, evidence, and human review; the prediction capability comes from the external model you connect. The offline fixture, model adapter, and full continuous screenshots are not yet fully verified in the current version. This page publishes an implementable evaluation contract and operating boundaries; it does not present them as an "out-of-the-box built-in virtual cell model." Evaluation task The 2026 Virtual Cell Challenge task is zero-shot cross-cell-background prediction: the model receives unperturbed baseline cells and CRISPRi knockdown target genes, and predicts post-perturbation expression profiles in cell backgrounds it has not seen before. For the official description, see Arc Institute's task overview. This tutorial focuses on four common risks: - The model sees the sealed ground truth before prediction, causing data leakage - Data, weight, or environment drift makes results impossible to rerun - The output shape is valid but gene order, value type, or labels are wrong - Only the overall score is reported, hiding consistent failures on specific backgrounds or perturbations Choose a path first Path Purpose Ground truth and scoring External effects --- --- --- --- A. Offline reproduction demo After preparing offline data, walk through prediction, sealing, local scoring, and rerun Requires independently sealed validation data prepared in advance; this site does not yet provide a verified fixture, and it is not the official held-out ground truth No upload by default; a small local CPU slice works B. VCC 2026 online path Assemble the official inputs and run pre-submission checks Run the official CLI preflight locally; final scoring happens on the official server Downloads, sign-ins, uploads, and submissions each require separate confirmation The two paths can share the prediction artifact contract, but they must not mix ground truth or scoring claims. When you cannot determine the path, stop. Workspace boundaries in SciForge Start by inspecting the protocol, data, model, and existing runs in the SciForge Files panel; do not launch a full prediction right away. Figure 1: The Files panel is used to check the current workspace and key inputs; this feature screenshot is not a completed benchmark run. Suggested layout: text virtual-cell-benchmark/ ├── protocol/ │ ├── evaluation-plan.md │ ├── data-contract.yaml │ └── split-manifest.json ├── data/ │ ├── inputs/ │ └── sealed-reference/ 仅路径 A ├── models/ │ ├── baseline/ │ └── external-adapter/ ├── scripts/ │ ├── validate_inputs.py │ ├── run_prediction.py │ ├── validate_prediction.py │ ├── evaluate_offline.py 仅路径 A │ └── analyze_failures.py └── runs/<run-id / ├── run-manifest.json ├── environment-lock. ├── logs/ ├── predictions/ ├── validation/ ├── metrics/ ├── figures/ └── dossier/ run-manifest.json is the core index. At minimum it records the path type, input hashes, code commit, model and weight hashes, environment, device, random seed, prediction hash, command, return code, and timestamp. Official output contract snapshot As of 2026-09-04, the full submission contract given by the official VCC CLI documentation includes: Contract item Official requirement Local check --- ---: --- Perturbations × cells per condition × backgrounds 300 × 400 × 3 Exact counts per background and per perturbation Total predicted cells 360,000 Check obs row count and duplicate keys Gene dimension 18,533 Gene set, order, and uniqueness Values Raw, non-negative integer counts Reject log-normalized, scaled, or negative values Control cells Should not be included Scan for non-targeting control labels Local preflight vcc prep --dry-run Save the CLI version, command, return code, and full output The official bundle downloaded at run time and the VCC CLI documentation are the final authority; if the CLI disagrees with this page, stop and update the protocol. Full task prompt text Please organize a reproducible virtual cell perturbation prediction evaluation in the current workspace. Goal: use unperturbed baseline cells and the given knockdown target genes to generate post-perturbation expression predictions, and pin the data, model, environment, runs, and results into a reviewable evidence chain. First determine the path from the workspace: - Path A: offline reproduction fixture, where local scoring can run after predictions are sealed. - Path B: official VCC 2026, where locally you only run contract checks and vcc prep --dry-run. - If you cannot determine the path, stop. Do not guess or mix the two paths. Execution requirements: 1. Inspect Git, data, model code, weights, environment, and evaluation scripts in read-only mode. 2. Generate an input inventory and hash manifest, separating what the model can see from what it cannot. 3. Before the first prediction, fix the metrics, aggregation rules, and failure conditions. 4. Run a small-sample dry run first, and check shape, gene order, labels, value types, device, and random seed. 5. Once that passes, generate predictions and record the command, arguments, environment, resources, return code, and prediction hash. 6. For path A, only read the sealed fixture after predictions are sealed. 7. For path B, run only vcc prep --dry-run; stop and confirm before any download, sign-in, upload, or submission. 8. Break down error by background, target gene, expression range, and metric component; do not report only the overall score. 9. Add the protocol, inputs, runs, predictions, validation, metrics, failures, and limitations to the Evidence DAG. 10. Rerun from a clean environment and generate a Research Dossier. Without my confirmation, do not download weights, install dependencies, sign in to external services, submit compute jobs, or upload data. If the input contract, gene space, scoring path, or evaluation script cannot be verified, stop immediately. Execution phases 1. Pre-register the protocol Create evaluation-plan.md before the first prediction, and freeze the data split, primary metrics, auxiliary metrics, aggregation rules, model-visible content, and stop conditions. The file time and Git record must predate the prediction output. 2. Pin the model and environment Record the code commit, weight hashes, license, environment lockfile, device, and random seed. Do not silently download new weights, swap models, or change data preprocessing. When you need an external GPU or a lab cluster, you can submit the job to your own remote environment through the Terminal; the remote side still uses the same output contract. 3. Small-sample dry run Check on the smallest slice: - Input and output shape - Gene ID set and order - Perturbation and background labels - Cells per condition - Non-negative integer counts - Sparse storage and peak memory - Device, random seed, and return code If any hard contract check fails, do not proceed to the full prediction. 4. Run and seal predictions As soon as the full prediction finishes, compute its hash, write it into the run manifest, and put the logs, return code, and resource information under the same run-id . An original run must not be overwritten by a later rerun. 5A. Offline scoring Only after predictions are sealed may you open the sealed fixture and score with the frozen evaluation script. If the reference was read by the model or an analysis script before sealing, mark that run as invalid and start over in a new workspace. 5B. Official preflight Run vcc prep --dry-run with the current official CLI. Passing the preflight does not mean you have submitted. Any sign-in, packaged upload, or formal submission is an external operation: show the target, files, size, and purpose, and get user confirmation. Stratified analysis and evidence review Divide the results into at least four layers: 1. Contract layer : whether files, shape, gene order, count type, and labels are correct. 2. Metric layer : report every component, the overall score, and the aggregation rules. 3. Stratified layer : check performance by background, perturbation, expression strength, and gene abundance. 4. Biology layer : label pathway or cell-state interpretations as hypotheses, and do not write scores directly as mechanistic conclusions. Recommended figures include component metrics, a dot plot stratified by background, perturbation-level error ranking, a differential expression comparison of observed versus predicted values, and an in-depth profile of at least one failure condition. Finally, in SciForge, organize the protocol, inputs, runs, predictions, metrics, failure cases, and limitations into the research dossier. Figure 3: The Research Dossier aggregates the research narrative, versions, confidence, and limitations; continuous screenshots from the same benchmark session still need to be captured before the case is officially published. When you must stop Problem Risk Handling --- --- --- Background labels unknown or swapped Predictions that look valid on the wrong background Check against a fixed mapping and stop immediately Same gene set but a different order Distorted metrics Check both the set and the order before prediction and scoring Output is normalized or scaled values Violates the raw count contract Verify non-negativity, integer values, and provenance; stop on failure Wrong cell count per perturbation Condition weights shift Verify exact counts per background and per perturbation Environment or weight drift Reruns are not comparable Create a new run-id and produce a difference report Path B preparing an upload Data leaves the local machine Show the target and files, and wait for user confirmation Completion criteria These items are the acceptance criteria for a later integration run; this page does not provide proof of a completed prediction, scoring, and rerun. - Path A/B is clear and the two are not mixed - The protocol predates the first prediction - Input, code, weight, environment, and prediction hashes are all present - All hard contracts pass in the dry run - The overall score and stratified failures are reported together - Rerun differences are recorded and explained - No external upload or submission happened without confirmation Next: Remote resources and collaboration.

en.title: ECCITE-seq cross-scale virtual cell evidence atlas
en.description: Review CRISPR perturbations, multimodal responses, figures, and evidence boundaries in SciForge.
en.body: ECCITE-seq cross-scale virtual cell evidence atlas This case organizes CRISPR perturbation, target annotation, pathways, transcriptional response, protein response, and cell fitness into an inspectable cross-scale evidence chain. SciForge manages the workspace, execution process, figures, evidence, and human review; it is not described as a built-in virtual cell predictor. The five screenshots below come from the current SciForge development build and open real artifacts in a separate cross-scale-data-demo workspace. They verify the artifact browsing path, but they do not claim that the current version has already completed every rerun from the same session. Research question After a designated target gene is CRISPR-perturbed in a specific cell background, what changes in transcription, protein, pathways, and cell fitness? Which data and methods support each conclusion? The case must answer both "what did we get" and "what can we still not say." Differential expression, protein response, or phenotypic association cannot automatically be promoted to a causal mechanism; cross-layer missingness must also be preserved as a result. Final delivery package The following are the acceptance targets for one complete case run. The current screenshots already show data, figure, and report browsing; same-session generation and review of the Evidence DAG, Research Checkpoint, and Research Dossier still need to be confirmed in an actual run. - Data sources, Git commit, file hashes, and environment baseline - A cross-scale perturbation review table that preserves controls and missing states - A set of versioned figures generated from verified derived tables - A quality audit report, run manifest, and artifact inventory - An Evidence DAG linking claims, data, scripts, figures, and limitations - A human-reviewed Research Checkpoint and Research Dossier Verified data snapshot The following is the static baseline of the public demo copy cross-scale-data-demo@0696755 . A real run must recompute these values instead of hard-coding the numbers into scripts. Item Snapshot Runtime check --- ---: --- Total rows in the review table 35 Recomputed from the final TSV Unique target genes 15 Deduplicated after excluding non-targeting controls Perturbation guides / non-targeting controls 27 / 8 Check perturbation type explicitly L1 target and L2 pathway annotation 27/35 Output unmatched identifiers L3 transcriptional response 27/35 measured Separate unmeasured from no significant response L4 protein response 35/35 measured State that the ADT panel has only 4 markers L5 fitness endpoint 27/35 The 8 missing entries must not be zero-filled Quality checks 42 pass, 1 warning The warning points to the L5 missing rate Delivered artifacts 22 Count data, results, figures, scripts, reports, and manifests by category Workspace and artifact contract text cross-scale-data-demo/ ├── data/final/case45_cross_scale_integrated_dataset.tsv ├── data/processed/case45_l0_l5/case45_p0_20260708T1015Z/ └── run-output/ ├── scripts/ │ ├── stage01_source_inventory.py │ ├── stage02_reconstruct_dataset.py │ ├── stage03_quality_audit.py │ ├── stage04_context_expansion.py │ ├── stage05_generate_figures.py │ └── stage06_write_report.py ├── datasets/ ├── results/ ├── figures/ └── reports/case45_local_demo_report.md Every Stage should record its inputs, outputs, return code, and stop conditions. If the quality audit fails, do not continue to conclusion figures; figures must come from verified derived tables; and the final report must not hide warnings or unverified items. Figure 1: SciForge keeps the case workspace and task on the left, while the Files panel on the right expands the run-output/figures artifact tree. Permissions and baseline before you start This case creates scripts, tables, figures, and research records, so it requires "Can modify working directory"; the read-only sandbox from Getting started does not apply. Before you start, you must: 1. Use a case copy that can be published and redistributed. 2. Check git status --short and record the baseline commit. 3. Inventory the input files and record hashes, sources, and license boundaries. 4. Review the agent plan, output paths, and dependency requirements. 5. Do not install dependencies or access unlisted external services without confirmation. Full task prompt text Please complete one reviewable ECCITE-seq cross-scale perturbation analysis in the current workspace. Research question: compare the designated target genes against non-targeting controls and inspect the evidence relationships among target annotation, pathways, transcriptional response, protein response, and cell fitness. Execution requirements: 1. Check Git status first, inventory the data, scripts, and existing artifacts, and do not overwrite the original files. 2. Present the plan, output paths, and data quality checks before you start writing. 3. Preserve non-targeting controls and missing data; do not automatically fill missing values with zeros. 4. Produce a traceable perturbation review table that lists the source and transformation for each row. 5. Generate cross-layer coverage figures and key response figures from the review table, and save the figure versions. 6. Link claims, data, methods, figures, and limitations into the Evidence DAG. 7. Generate a Research Checkpoint and a Research Dossier, and list the causal conclusions that are not yet supported. Unless I explicitly allow it, do not install dependencies, do not access unlisted external services, and do not modify the raw data. Mark any data or conclusion you cannot verify as "unverified". Phase 1: Freeze sources and inspect the data The agent first inventories the data, scripts, and existing artifacts, then checks perturbation labels, controls, cell backgrounds, measured modalities, and missing values. The completion signal here is not a one-line "checks passed," but an inventory, a hash manifest, and a quality audit report you can open. Check specifically: - Non-targeting controls are not lost in a join or filter - missing is not conflated with the numeric value 0 - "Not measured" and "measured with no significant response" are expressed separately - Every external annotation records the provider, query conditions, and access date Figure 2: Viewing L0–L5 coverage and measurement status in SciForge; the workspace and task context remain in frame. Phase 2: Assemble the perturbation review table Connect perturbations, target annotation, pathways, and multimodal responses into one row-by-row traceable table. Recompute the row count, unique target gene count, control count, and per-layer coverage, and output the list of unmatched identifiers. If you only have a ready-made derived table without the complete raw counts, you must downgrade the task to "a traceable review of the existing derived results," and you must not claim that the full differential expression analysis was redone. Phase 3: Generate and inspect versioned figures All figures are generated from derived tables that passed the audit, and each records its input hash, script, parameters, and figure version. The same inputs and recipe should rebuild the same result. Figure 3: The file preview shows both the figure and the actual artifact path, so you can trace a result back to its input. When reading L3 and L4, do not give priority to the layer that "matches expectations better." A direction mismatch may come from time scale, measurement noise, or the coverage limits of the 4-marker ADT panel, and it should be preserved as a cross-layer separation result. Figure 4: Causal readiness, L3/L4 overlap, and the L5 effect distribution are inspected together in SciForge; this figure cannot support a causal claim on its own. Phase 4: Review the evidence and lock down delivery Connect each key claim to the original records, derived table, method script, and figure. Counter-evidence, missingness, and limitations should also become evidence nodes rather than being deleted from the final narrative. After the review passes: 1. Open Changes to verify the write scope. 2. Save an Artifact Version for the figures and key files. 3. Create a Research Checkpoint. 4. Record the research question, inputs, methods, results, limitations, and rerun procedure in the Research Dossier. Figure 5: The first screen of the final report shows stage status, the data baseline, the quality audit, and the artifact count. Conclusion writing template text Supported claims: - Which perturbation affected which layer of measurement, in which cell background? - Which original records, derived tables, methods, and figures directly support it? Candidate explanations: - Which pathway or mechanism could explain the result? - What assumptions does it depend on, and what validation is still missing? Claims that cannot be supported: - Why is the current data insufficient to support causal, generalized, or clinical conclusions? - What data, experiments, or independent reproduction is needed next? Failure paths and recovery Problem Wrong approach Correct handling --- --- --- L5 missing Fill with 0 and include in the average Keep the missing flag and report total N and evaluable N separately L3/L4 direction mismatch Keep only the layer that matches expectations better Keep the separated result and check the time scale and marker coverage Audit raises an error Keep plotting and write the Dossier Stop at the quality stage and rerun from the affected Stage after fixing External annotation unavailable Silently switch provider Use a frozen snapshot or stop, and flag freshness Raw counts incomplete Claim the full analysis was redone Downgrade to a traceable review of the existing derived table Completion criteria Use the following to accept your own run; they do not mean this page has already completed all continuous verification. - Baseline commit, input hashes, and environment records are available - The 35-row review table, 15 target genes, and 8 controls can be recomputed - Missing states and warnings are not hidden - Figures trace back to verified derived tables and generation scripts - Key claims have an evidence, counter-evidence, or unresolved status - Checkpoint, Dossier, and Git changes are reviewed together Related feature: Evidence & Reproducibility.

en.title: Anchored Comments
en.description: Select a piece of text, leave a comment, and come back to discuss and check it in place.
en.body: Anchored Comments Select a piece of text in a research record to leave a question, a suggested change, or review feedback on it. The comment keeps the original text and its position, so you can check back later. Add a comment 1. In Extensions & marketplace, install and enable a compatible Anchored Comments plugin. 2. Open Research record , and drag to select text within a single entry. 3. Click Add comment , and check the original text and target shown in the panel. 4. Write your feedback and click Save . Discuss selection opens a chat draft that carries the selected text. To save it as a comment, use Add comment . If the panel already holds unsaved content, a new selection asks whether to keep or replace the draft. View, edit, and delete You can ask the agent to list or read the comments in the current workspace, and to update an existing thread. The panel is mainly for creating new comments; to edit existing content, use the plugin's tools. Deleting a comment requires confirmation. Comments are stored in the workspace and do not change the commented source file. After you switch projects, select the content you want to comment on again. Screenshots and feedback A screenshot is a separate action; saving text does not take one automatically. The plugin can save a screenshot of the current app view only when the host provides that feature and allows capture. Before capturing, check for accounts, tokens, or other sensitive information. Submitting feedback to an external service also needs separate confirmation. If no feedback service is configured, comments can only be saved and discussed locally. Tips - After the original text changes, re-check the quotation and its position. - Comments belong to the current workspace. Before sharing a project, check the comments and screenshots for content you do not want to share. - The current plugin version is 0.2.1 . For installation requirements and version notes, see Version & Compatibility. Related: Agent workflows, Plugin license terms.

en.title: Artifact Versions
en.description: Save immutable versions of individual artifacts such as charts and data, and compare or restore them at any time.
en.body: Artifact Versions Artifact Versions gives each artifact in a workspace a stable identity and records every save as an immutable version. It answers the question "which revision of this chart or dataset am I on, and can I return to a specific one?" It sits after analysis produces output and before evidence organization and delivery; research context is still recorded by Research Checkpoints, and claim-to-source relationships are handled by Evidence DAG. How to open it - Entry: the Artifacts area of the workbench research summary lists recent artifacts; select a specific item, then view versions in the Research panel on the right. - Scope: a single artifact in the current workspace, such as a chart, dataset, log, or code file. - Prerequisite: an agent or production plugin has already committed the artifact as a version, and the session is bound to a workspace. What you can do What you want to do How to do it Output --- --- --- Pin a produced output Have the agent or a tool integrated with the artifact versioning service commit a new version An immutable version and a current pointer Ingest large files Submit bytes through staged upload (begin → append → seal, abort on failure) A content-addressed snapshot Compare two versions Select exact versions in the Versions area of the research dossier and compare them Differences in content, metadata, and dependencies Return to an older version Select a historical version and restore it as a new version A new current version; the old version is retained Package for exchange Select an exact version in the research dossier and export a Bundle; verify it before importing A portable bundle and verification result Typical workflow 1. Generate a chart or dataset in a task and confirm that the file is in the current workspace. 2. Have the agent commit the artifact; add dependencies and access policy if needed. 3. Open the exact version in the Research panel and check the content digest and dependencies. 4. After changes, commit again and compare the old and new versions; restore as a new version if needed. 5. Before delivery, select the exact version in the research dossier and export a Bundle, then verify and import it in the target workspace. Inputs, outputs, and permissions - Reads: artifact metadata, version history, and snapshot bytes in the current workspace; restricted versions are filtered by access policy. - Writes: the version index, content-addressed objects, and lifecycle events; restoring only adds a version and never rewrites history. - Approval or external effects: Bundle export writes a bundle file, and import installs version records; when export is triggered from the research dossier, the UI asks for confirmation first. - What it does not do: judge scientific conclusions, generate claim-to-source relationships, or fall back to "latest" when no exact version is specified. Known limitations - Content appears only if a task has actually committed artifacts. Scientific Figures maintains its own figure history and does not automatically commit it here; register an artifact version separately when you need to connect the two. - Snapshot bytes are stored by content address; reference-based versions re-verify workspace files on read, so moves, content changes, or missing files surface as source status. - Bundle export requires explicitly selecting a non-empty artifact or version; if any version in the closure is invisible or export-prohibited, the entire export fails; import rejects incomplete dependencies, non-linear history, duplicate sequence numbers, circular references, or corrupted objects. - Staged upload transfers data in chunks with a 4 MiB limit per chunk; an incomplete, expired stage cannot accept further appends. - Each version carries an immutable access policy; reads, comparisons, restores, and imports all enforce the same policy, and restricted versions are not loosened by the history UI. Related pages - Evidence & Reproducibility: the group overview and the recommended record chain. - Research Dossier: view, compare, restore, and export exact versions from the dossier. - Evidence DAG: use versions as the evidence and sources behind a claim. - Git Checkpoints: pin the Git state of the whole workspace rather than a single artifact. - Workspaces and sessions: how a workspace scopes artifacts. Implementation basis: @sciforge/domain-artifact-versions v1.4.0.

en.title: Automation and scheduled tasks
en.description: Use scheduled tasks to repeat a single Agent instruction, or use Create Loop to organize multi-step flows.
en.body: Automation and scheduled tasks First verify in an ordinary session that the task completes correctly, then turn it into an automation. Define the output path and the operations that need confirmation up front, so that scheduled repeats do not overwrite files or submit twice. Automation has two entry points: Scheduled tasks is a built-in scheduling capability of the app, not a domain extension; Create Loop is a built-in flow tool for multi-node orchestration. Choose which one Need Entry point --- --- Run a single AI instruction daily, once, at an interval, or manually Scheduled tasks (this page) Connect AI tasks, conditions, HTTP requests, approvals, and subflows Create Loop Create a scheduled task Open Scheduled tasks from the left, click New task , and configure the name, instruction, model, reasoning effort, run time, and workspace in order. Figure 1: A scheduled task puts the task content, model, schedule, and runtime environment in a single configuration table. An instruction suitable for validation: Check the current workspace for newly appeared experiment logs and produce a summary of no more than three items. Do not modify the original logs; save the output to the prearranged reports directory. Scheduled tasks require SciForge to keep running and the computer to be awake at the trigger time. "Keep awake" only prevents suspension while a task is running; it cannot wake a computer that is already asleep. Create a Loop When you need multiple steps, open Create Loop from the right toolbar or More tools . For full instructions, see Create Loop (multi-step flows); the shortest path is: 1. Create a Loop and add AI task, condition, HTTP request, or manual approval nodes. 2. Define the input, output, and failure handling for each node. 3. Test a single node first, then run the whole flow manually. 4. Enable schedule triggers, Webhooks, or Agent hooks only after validation. When a manual approval node pauses, it depends on the current app's in-memory state; restarting the app loses that paused run. For important flows, make node outputs repeatable and keep idempotency identifiers and run records. Automation acceptance - Workspace and output paths are explicit - Runtime, model, and Skill are fixed - The shortest task has already succeeded in an ordinary session - Individual nodes and the whole flow have each passed testing - External requests, writes, and credential use have approval boundaries - Recent results, errors, and recovery methods can be found When automation fails, do not start by increasing the retry count; first open the session and node results for the most recent run and determine whether the error will repeatedly produce external effects.

en.title: Biology Room
en.description: Pin sequences, structures, genome tracks, and annotations into a traceable workspace room.
en.body: Biology Room Biology Room is the room submodule of the built-in @sciforge/domain-biology-workbench 1.1.3 . It shares one domain package with Life Science Preview, ships with the app, and needs no marketplace install or plugin enablement; there is no runtime-plugin takeover path. For how versions are quoted, see Version & Compatibility. Biology Room is a workspace object for biological samples or experimental material: it puts the sequences, structures, genome tracks, and annotations needed for viewing, annotating, and handoff into a single versioned room. It has no separate rendering panel today, so file contents still appear in file preview; the room manages assets, selections, view state, and history. Opening it - Entry point: an Agent invokes a Biology Room capability in a session to create or open a room; files inside the room are viewed through file preview. - Applies to: biological files and room manifests in the current workspace; paths must be workspace-relative. - Prerequisite: the workspace is writable; asset extensions are supported; when an index is referenced, the index lives in the same workspace as the source file. What it can do What you want to do How to do it Output --- --- --- Create a room Give a title and optionally attach a first batch of assets Initial room manifest and revision 1 Open or create from a file Pass in one workspace file; reuse an existing room that already contains that file A new room, or the manifest of an existing room Add and manage assets Add or remove assets, or switch the current asset, against the current revision A new revision; asset fingerprint, format, modality, and readiness status Record selections and annotations Save sequence, structure, or genome selections and view state, and bind annotation anchors Structured selections, view state, and annotations stored by anchor Refresh and roll back Refresh asset fingerprints; view history and restore a revision Updated revision, orphaned annotation markers, and history events Typical workflow 1. List existing rooms first and check whether a room already contains the target file, to avoid creating duplicates. 2. Open or create a room from the file; verify the returned path, format, SHA-256, and index fingerprint. 3. Commit a set of changes against the current revision, using dry-run mode first to see whether there are changes and warnings. 4. After applying the changes, read the room again and verify the revision, asset readiness, and annotation anchors. 5. Refresh the room after source files change; to roll back, view history first, then restore the older revision to produce a new revision number. Inputs, outputs, and permissions - Read: FASTA/GenBank, PDB/mmCIF, and GFF3/BED/VCF files in the workspace, optionally with .fai , .gzi , .tbi , and .csi indexes; up to 4 indexes per asset. - Write: room manifests, revision snapshots, and event logs, stored in the room directory under .sciforge/biology/rooms/ in the workspace; source files are referenced read-only. - Approval or external effects: room writes touch workspace metadata only and do not trigger approval; put human confirmation before dry-run review, cascading asset removal, and restoring an old revision. - What it will not do: modify or delete source files, perform alignment, variant calling, or structural computation, or provide real-time multi-user collaboration; removing an asset removes only the room reference. Known limitations - Narrower support than Life Science Preview: no FASTQ, GTF, omics matrices, imaging, or spectra; gzip covers only FASTA, GFF, BED, and VCF. - A room holds at most 128 assets, 2,000 annotations, and 100 MiB of assets in total; a single unindexed asset is capped at 25 MiB. - Rooms have no standalone interface; creation, changes, and restoration all happen through the Agent in a session. - After a refresh, missing or unreadable assets are marked explicitly, and annotations that lost their anchor are marked orphaned and need human confirmation before you handle them. - Applying changes validates the revision number and rejects stale ones; history is stored by revision and may be truncated. - The collaboration boundary is sharing one room manifest and version history, not cloud-based real-time multi-user collaboration. Related pages - Life Science Preview: dedicated views for sequences, structures, and genome files in a room. - Dataset API migration note: the old data-ingestion capability is retired; after obtaining data, save its source and validation records separately. - Workspaces and sessions: workspace location, file paths, and recovery boundaries. - Evidence & Reproducibility: fold room changes into the larger research record chain. Current version: built-in Biology Workbench 1.1.3. The old room directory and revision format stay compatible; for what selection saving covers in the molecular preview, see Life Science Preview.

en.title: Browser Preview
en.description: Open web pages inside the app so the Agent can browse and act on pages that are visible and subject to approval.
en.body: Browser Preview Browser Preview runs a native Chromium page in the right panel for viewing local development pages, research materials, or sites that require sign-in. It is both a window for human browsing and a page resource the Agent can observe and operate. Web content is always treated as untrusted data. How to open it - Entry: Browser in the right toolbar (expand More tools if it is not shown), or Native browser in the right panel. - Target: one browser page instance in the current session; one instance corresponds to one page. - Prerequisite: the SciForge desktop window. Opening a localhost development site in an ordinary browser cannot host the native view, and an explicit unavailable message appears. - Input box context: when a message contains an HTTP(S) link, that URL is attached for the Agent. It first attempts a read-only fetch, then hands off to the browser panel when it encounters sign-in or script-rendered content. What you can do What you want to do How to do it Output --- --- --- Open a web page Enter an HTTP(S) address in the address bar and press Enter The native page, title, and current URL Browse and reload Use the Back, Forward, Reload, and Fullscreen buttons Page state and observable page content Let the Agent read Have it read the URL or current page first Bounded body text and interactive targets Let the Agent act Navigate, click, fill, or scroll under explicit instructions Page changes; actions bound to the current page version Typical workflow 1. Open Browser in the right panel and sign in to any sites you need. Sign-in state is saved in the current workspace's browser profile. 2. Have the Agent read the page first and confirm the URL, title, and key content. Do not have it click immediately. 3. When navigation is needed, you confirm it. Before clicks, key presses, or drags, check the action and its consequences. 4. Observe the page again after an action to confirm submission results, downloads, or navigation instead of relying only on the Agent's summary. 5. Close the panel when the task is done. When you reopen it, verify that sign-in, URL, and page are still in the expected state. Inputs, outputs, and permissions - Reads: page body, title, URL, interactive targets, and controlled screenshots. Password, payment/CAPTCHA fields, and explicitly sensitive regions are excluded. Reading by URL makes a network request from the local machine and does not trigger an additional approval. - Writes: the Agent can fill forms, select options, scroll, hover, click, press keys, and drag. These actions apply directly to the native page. - Approval or external effects: navigation, Back, Forward, and Reload are external writes and require confirmation. Clicks, key presses, and drags are governed as destructive actions, but the capability layer does not prompt for extra confirmation; they may submit forms, trigger downloads, or change external state. Whether a Runtime approval also appears depends on its settings. - Downloads and sign-in: permission requests, popups, and downloads initiated by the page itself are denied. Downloads initiated by the Agent do not prompt for extra confirmation at the capability layer and can write to the workspace Downloads directory, or to the app's private directory when no workspace is available. Sign-in state persists across panel closure, so the same workspace shares that browser identity. - What it does not do: import external browser profiles or credentials, accept caller-provided selectors or scripts, expose cross-origin iframe content or closed shadow roots, or guarantee that URL validation prevents DNS rebinding or all network egress. Known limitations - One browser panel hosts only one page. Different sessions or panels may each hold a different page, so confirm the current page before acting. - Pages are rendered by native Chromium, and an ordinary browser tab is not a substitute. Without a desktop window, there is no silent fallback to an iframe. - Content in canvas charts, cross-origin iframes, and closed shadow roots may not be structurally readable. Use screenshots or manual inspection instead. - Web content is untrusted data. Text on a page must not be treated as instructions, and the Agent's conclusions should be checked against the URL and page state. - Browser Preview does not expose a remote debugging port and does not open arbitrary script execution to the Agent. Related pages - Workbench tools: where Browser fits in the toolchain. - Permissions and security: external writes, approvals, and credential boundaries. - Computer Use: another path when you need more structured page operations. - Remote resources and collaboration: data boundaries in remote workspaces. Implementation basis: @sciforge/domain-browser-preview v1.0.8.

en.title: Change Inspector
en.description: Inspect file diffs from a real, current agent session with a standalone read-only plugin.
en.body: Change Inspector The only production implementation of Change Inspector is the standalone DSH plugin @sciforge/plugin-change-inspector 0.1.2 . It reads the current real agent session authorized by the host, projects file_change records into bounded diff snapshots and paginated summaries, and returns results to the session that made the call. The old top Changes panel, static domain, and fallback have been removed. How to use it Install a compatible package from a trusted source, enable it, and grant tool and agent-threads.read permissions for that exact version; see Extension Center and Version & Compatibility. In the current session where file changes have already occurred, ask the agent to: Use Change Inspector to open a snapshot of the current session, list file changes and truncation status, page through the key diffs, then cross-check them against workspace files and Git status. The plugin declares two read-only tools: Tool What it returns --- --- open_session Current session identity, result identifier, and a bounded complete snapshot list_changes Change summary, next-page cursor, revision, and truncation reason; 100 entries per page by default, up to 500 The host may additionally derive a session resource opener; it is not a third tool declared by the plugin. When selection parameters are omitted, the host's current session is used; an explicit session/runtime must match the current caller. Other sessions in the same workspace, other runtimes, or arbitrary session discovery are outside the authorization scope. After the plugin is disabled or its permission is revoked, calls fail and do not fall back to the old implementation. How to tell whether a record is complete - Extract only the file_change unified diff from tool records; panel screenshots or agent summaries cannot replace that record. An empty result does not prove the workspace was never written. - A snapshot holds at most 5,000 changes and 256 KiB after serialization; when the limit is exceeded, the contiguous newest suffix is kept. A single complete patch is capped at 64 KiB, and a single patch summary in pagination is capped at 1 KiB. - Check patchBytes , patchTruncated , truncated , and truncationReasons . Trailing whitespace and LF/CRLF line endings are preserved in untruncated raw patches; truncated output cannot be used for complete file reconstruction. - A cursor is bound to the session and revision. After subsequent edits or if the cursor is rejected, re-read from the first page without a cursor; read-only pagination itself should not change the revision. Permissions and verification boundaries The plugin does not write files, roll back changes, save checkpoints, or make network requests; its only data source is the host-authenticated real agent thread aggregate. Tool inputs cannot inject recorded sessions or fixtures. Existing local app acceptance for 0.1.2 covers a real two-turn trailing-whitespace difference, stable pagination, and partial rejection and failure recovery; other permission timings and boundaries are covered by targeted automation. Source tests, real subprocess fixtures, local app acceptance, signed artifacts, and public marketplace release are different forms of evidence and cannot substitute for one another; this page does not claim that all platforms or all failure scenarios have passed. Retained historical UI screenshot: it shows the old panel, not the current 0.1.2 plugin entry point or acceptance evidence. Related: Evidence & Reproducibility, Git Checkpoints, Permissions & security, Plugin licenses.

en.title: Collaboration guide
en.description: Starting from requirements and task assignment, complete member acceptance, human review, delivery adoption, and project close-out.
en.body: Collaboration guide The owner writes clear requirements and confirms the division of work. Members accept tasks, execute them in their own SciForge, review drafts, and submit. Finally the owner adopts the result. Tasks that hand off to one another use the files already adopted upstream. This page reflects the interface as of 2026-11-06. For differences in installed versions, see Version & Compatibility. Open a collaboration project 1. Expand the left sidebar and complete cloud sign-in and device connection in the account area at the bottom. 2. In the sidebar's collaboration area, open a project, My work , or Inbox . If you cannot see the project tree, expand the sidebar first. 3. In an ordinary session, confirm the Runtime and model respond before starting a collaboration task. Each member uses their own cloud account. Project requirements, discussions, result notes, and submitted files go to the collaboration service; an ordinary local workspace is not synced as a whole directory. Do not put model keys or sign-in credentials into any of these. Once a project is selected, there are five tabs at the top: Tab Purpose --- --- Board See tasks and the progress of acceptance, assignment, review, and adoption Members See project members; invite or manage members according to your current role Requirements Edit goals, inputs, work modules, and acceptance criteria, and confirm requirements Shared files See shared material, sealed task deliveries, and project results Project info See the project description, status, and available management actions 1. The owner prepares and confirms requirements 1. In the collaboration project area, use + to create a project and fill in a name. 2. Open Requirements and edit Goals & deliverables and Inputs & boundaries . State the data sources, final files, how acceptance works, and the actions that must not be performed. 3. Click Save requirements and wait for the work modules to be completed. On failure, read the message, check the model configuration, then use Regenerate . 4. Check each module's goal, inputs, outputs, dependencies, and acceptance criteria. When all are correct, click Confirm requirements . 5. Invite members under Members . Invitees enter from the inbox or the project invitation prompt, read the requirements, and accept the invitation. For example: "B counts the total samples and submits a report; C continues the comparison using the report B had adopted. The report must include the method, validation results, and limitations." Also provide inputs the members can actually read. Historical demo screenshot (kept when checked on 2026-11-06; capture date not recorded): shows work modules and dependencies. For current navigation, follow the five tabs on this page. 2. Check assignments and blocking reasons On the board, the owner opens a task and checks the executor and upstream dependencies. Depending on the task's current state, choose a member and Assign task or Reassign , or Change assignee or Withdraw assignment for an assignment not yet accepted. A module with dependencies waits until its upstream result is adopted. The interface keeps the assign entry and shows the reason, with the button disabled. Finish the upstream review first. If a task is still unassigned after requirements are confirmed, or assignment failed and no member is available, the owner needs to pick an executor or handle the to-do as prompted. Do not treat a task waiting to be assigned as already running. 3. Members decide whether to accept Members can see incoming assignments from Inbox, My work, a board task card, or task details . Read the goal, file requirements, dependencies, and validity period first, then choose: Action Result --- --- Accept task Confirms you take the task; it runs once your local Runtime is ready, or you are prompted to recover it Ignore Handles the current assignment, and the task is removed from your related lists; it is not the same as dismissing a notice bar Decline Explicitly declines the current assignment; the owner rearranges it according to the project state Go by the buttons actually available; an assignment that has expired or been handled cannot be accepted again. Dismissing the assignment reminder on the board does not perform "Ignore" for you. After accepting, use the task session to see run progress and tool calls. 4. Handle agent questions and action confirmations When a task needs more information, the designated member answers in the task details. If a request involves actions such as modifying files, writing to external systems, or deleting, first read the specific action, its scope of impact, the request version, and its validity period, write a decision note, then click Approve this action or Decline this action . Only the designated member can decide, and an expired request must wait to be refreshed. After submitting a decision, check the receipt and later task progress; whether the action completed depends on what actually ran. An ordinary discussion message does not replace action approval. 5. Members review the draft and submit 1. When execution finishes, open the delivery draft, preview the required files, and check the content. 2. Edit the Result note , stating what was actually done, the check results, and limitations. 3. To add material, click Add material : choose this run's output from Task files , or use Upload from this computer . Extra material does not replace the required files. 4. To have the AI revise, go to the task session through Ask AI to revise . 5. Check the file list and click Submit . In the confirmation window, check the version, note, and files, then confirm the submission. While submitting, wait for a clear result from device verification, signing, and file upload. If a system secure-storage authorization prompt appears, handle it yourself. On success, a versioned delivery snapshot is created and waits for the owner's review. This version cannot be edited in place; a revision creates a new version. One delivery can hold at most 20 files, no more than 200 MiB in total; each attached file is at most 100 MiB. Required files may also have task-specific format and size requirements, so follow the submission window's prompts. Historical demo screenshot (kept when checked on 2026-11-06; capture date not recorded): shows how the result note, required files, and extra material relate. Historical demo screenshot (kept when checked on 2026-11-06; capture date not recorded): the upload stage still waits for the final submission receipt. 6. The owner reviews and hands off downstream On the board, open a task pending confirmation, preview this version's files, and read the result note against the acceptance criteria. To ask for more, use Request revision and write specific feedback; the member revises, rechecks, and submits a new version. When the requirements are met, click Adopt , and the task moves to Completed. History keeps older snapshots, so check the current version when reviewing. Only after the upstream is adopted can a downstream task continue to assignment; downstream execution uses the files of the adopted version. Historical demo screenshot (kept when checked on 2026-11-06; capture date not recorded): a formal revision uses "Request revision"; discussion is for communication. Historical demo screenshot (kept when checked on 2026-11-06; capture date not recorded): a new delivery keeps the record of the previous version. 7. View shared files and close out Shared files lists project files by source and version, and lets you preview submitted content. Upload file here is currently unavailable and shows the reason. To submit material with a task, go back to Add material in the delivery draft; do not wait for an upload to succeed on the Shared files page. After all modules are adopted, the owner checks the results and limitations, then uses the Close project entry to confirm completion and waits for signing and the server result. Historical demo screenshot (kept when checked on 2026-11-06; capture date not recorded): shows how module adoption relates to project close-out; it is not an acceptance record for the current release package. Board status at a glance Column Meaning Next step --- --- --- Inbox The module has not been assigned, perhaps waiting on a dependency or manual assignment The owner checks the blocking reason and executor To start Assigned, waiting for the member to accept The member reads, then accepts, ignores, or declines In progress Running, waiting for a human answer, or the member is reviewing the draft Check task details and handle the current request Pending confirmation A delivery has been submitted The owner reviews, requests revision, or adopts Completed The module's result is adopted The owner closes the project once all modules are done On a network interruption, submission failure, or signature error, keep the draft first, check sign-in and device status, and after recovery check whether a submission record already exists before retrying as prompted. Continue reading: Pasilla three-person collaboration case, Identity & Access, Runtime & models.

en.title: Computer Use
en.description: Let supported Runtimes safely operate graphical interfaces through the local Backend.
en.body: Computer Use Computer Use lets supported Runtimes operate graphical interfaces on the desktop through a local Backend, turning observation, clicks, and input into governed MCP tools. It is suited to steps that must go through a UI and have no stable API. Every state-changing action requires a confirmed invocation. How to open it - Entry: Settings → AI assistant → Computer use . Turn on the main switch and select the Runtimes allowed to use it. - Target: the graphical interface target bound to and authorized for the current session. The current implementation uses a browser CDP backend to handle browser pages and Electron embedded pages. - Prerequisite: the local Computer Use Backend is running. On macOS, screen recording and Accessibility permissions are also required. - Connection: SciForge starts a managed MCP Server and provides bounded tools to Codex/Claude Code. No manual MCP command configuration is needed. Figure 1: The Computer Use entry, Backend status, and system permissions on the Settings page. What you can do What you want to do How to do it Output --- --- --- Check availability View Backend and system permission status on the Settings page An available or unavailable status, with no silent fallback Observe the target Have the Agent read the current target and interactive elements first A bounded page or target observation Perform one action Click, type, press a key, or scroll under explicit instructions A structured action result and page version Stop or release Stop the current task or release the session In-flight actions canceled and bindings cleaned up Typical workflow 1. Enable Computer Use in Settings and select only the Runtimes this task needs. 2. Check Backend status and confirm in macOS System Settings that screen recording and Accessibility are authorized. 3. In the session, state the target page, the outcome you want, the stop conditions, and prohibited actions. 4. Have the Agent observe first, then perform actions step by step. Every state-changing call requires your confirmation. 5. Release the session when done and verify the result in the UI. Do not treat a successful tool return as confirmation of the business result. Inputs, outputs, and permissions - Reads: structured observations of the current target, interactive elements, and bounded screenshots. Read-only queries do not require confirmation. - Writes: UI actions such as clicks, typing, key presses, and scrolling. Every change must be bound to one trusted, confirmed invocation. - Approval or external effects: actions such as signing in, authorizing, sending, uploading, purchasing or paying, deleting, and submitting official results must be confirmed by the user at execution time. A confirmation covers only that call and does not automatically authorize later actions of the same kind. - Data boundary: screens and observation results may contain account details, patient information, or unpublished data and should be treated as sensitive. Do not ask the Agent to fill in passwords, verification codes, or payment information. - What it does not do: bypass system permissions, keep operating after the turn ends, promise automation for arbitrary desktop apps, or switch to another backend when the Backend is unavailable. Known limitations - The current execution backend is browser CDP, so targets are limited to browser pages and Electron embedded pages (for example, Browser Preview). It is not a general automation tool for arbitrary desktop apps. - It requires the local Backend and a supported Runtime connection. When the Backend is unavailable, it reports an explicit error and does not silently degrade. - Only Codex and Claude Code are supported. Other Runtimes do not receive this tool set. - Screenshots and observation results are treated as untrusted and potentially sensitive by default. Redact them before export. - Bindings for the turn are reclaimed when the session ends. Computer Use is not intended for unattended, long-running automation. Related pages - Permissions and security: Computer Use system permissions and confirmation of key actions. - Skills, MCP, and Extensions: the differences between MCP, Skills, and plugins. - Browser Preview: the main source of pages that Computer Use currently operates. - Workbench tools: how tools divide responsibilities and how to use them. Implementation basis: @sciforge/domain-computer-use v1.0.1.

en.title: Content Space
en.description: Connect external content services, and see the notebook and shared-file entry points currently supported.
en.body: Content Space Content Space provides a single entry point to external content services. The current SiYuan connection can list notebooks; whether you can go on to browse, read, write, or transfer depends on what the connected service actually supports. Content stays in the original service. How to open it - Entry: Content Space in the right panel. Shared files on the full Collaboration page uses the same entry point. Shared files currently has no direct upload button. - Target: containers, regular files, and Provider-native documents from connected Providers. Currently, only SiYuan notebooks can be listed. - Prerequisite: install and connect a Provider that declares the relevant operation family. Connection usually requires the service address and account/token; Content Space does not read credentials. OpenContent has been retired; the only Provider currently available to users is SiYuan, and it declares notebook discovery only. What you can do You can currently choose SiYuan notebooks. The other operations in the table below need separate support from the service provider and must not be treated as currently available features; in particular, you cannot upload files directly through the Shared files entry. What you want to do How to do it Output --- --- --- Select a space or container Select the root or a directory of a connected Provider in Content Space; SiYuan lists notebooks that are not closed A read-only container reference Browse and locate files List container entries and open them by exact resource reference A file or container view Upload or download regular files After the Provider declares transfer operations, copy between the container and the workspace through a Host-restricted transfer A file copy subject to Host transfer limits Open or write Provider-native documents After the Provider declares native document operations, execute against the target document and version A document in the Provider Manage shared spaces and members Available only when the Provider declares Administration A member change receipt Typical workflow 1. Install and connect the Provider first. The connection binds the current user to a specific Provider instance and cannot be copied for use by another user. 2. Open Content Space and select a Provider and container. SiYuan currently lists only notebooks that are not closed; selecting one returns a read-only container reference. 3. To read or write SiYuan documents, go to the SiYuan Notes page, or have the Agent use SiYuan's search, read, and write capabilities. 4. When the interface says an operation is not yet supported, use the original service's own entry point. If the connection is no longer valid, reconnect first. Inputs, outputs, and permissions - Reads: Provider instances, containers, file metadata, and the readiness level declared by the Provider. Provider credentials are not read or displayed. - Writes: files, native documents, or membership in the Provider. Locally, only non-secret references and the current user's connection binding are kept. - Approval or external effects: ordinary non-destructive writes can run within authorized resources. Native document and extension operations declared destructive, member changes, and any destructive operation require human confirmation every time and cannot reuse the previous approval. - What it does not do: replace a Provider's native ACL with Project member permissions, automatically fall back to another Provider after a binding becomes invalid, or treat a raw ID as authorization. Known limitations - OpenContent has been retired : space and member management, upload and download, and native documents are no longer served by an OpenContent Provider. When no service supports an operation, the interface says it is unavailable. - The current SiYuan Provider declares notebook discovery only; other operations return blocked_by_contract . The local mock Provider is for testing only and is not a user feature. - The readiness level is evidence only and does not guarantee that a given call will be allowed. Every call also checks the current identity, authorization, audience, platform, transfer limits, and binding status. - Immutable artifact references ( ArtifactReference ) require proof of immutable retention and exact-version reads. Issuance is blocked when those conditions are not currently met. - Shared container members and Cloud Project members are two separate identity boundaries. Provider membership does not grant Project permissions. Related pages - SiYuan Notes: the currently installed Content Space Provider and its capability boundaries. - Collaboration: the relationship between Shared files and task delivery files. - Permissions and security: general rules for external writes and per-operation confirmation. - Feature status and limitations: how current capability status is defined. Implementation basis: @sciforge/domain-content-space v5.0.4.

en.title: Create Loop (multi-step workflows)
en.description: Chain AI, conditions, HTTP, and human approvals in multi-node workflows.
en.body: Create Loop (multi-step workflows) Create Loop breaks a task into multiple inspectable steps. It sits above session execution: AI nodes generate or decide, condition and data-processing nodes control the path, HTTP nodes connect external systems, subflows reuse another Loop, and human approvals determine whether key actions proceed. Before using it, confirm that the models, network, and tools the chosen nodes need are available, and run the whole flow through in your current environment. How to open it - Entry: Create Loop in the right toolbar (expand More tools if it is not shown). Edit nodes on the canvas; the right panel shows settings for the current Loop. - Target: one Loop in the current workspace. Definitions and run records are stored in local domain state. - Prerequisite: AI nodes need an available Runtime and model, HTTP nodes need network access, and schedules and local webhooks are triggered by the app process, so the app must remain running. A Loop can be started with manual Run once , a schedule, a webhook, or an Agent hook.
