What you can do What you want to do How to do it Output --- --- --- Chain a multi-step task Add AI agent task , LLM generation , Condition , HTTP request , human approval, subflow, and other nodes from the left node panel, then connect them A Loop you can save Branch on data Organize inputs and outputs with Condition, Switch, Merge, Filter, Loop, and similar nodes Explicit data flow between nodes Validate before going live Use Test node with mock upstream input for a single node, then Run once for the whole Loop Node results and run logs Stop at key points Add a Human Approval node, set the title, instruction, and timeout, then Approve/Reject on the card or in the run drawer Controlled release Trigger automatically Configure a schedule, webhook, or Agent hook Scheduled, external, or event-driven triggers Typical workflow 1. Open Create Loop from the right toolbar or More tools , name it, and confirm the working directory. AI, image, and code nodes all use that directory. 2. Add trigger and task nodes and connect them in execution order. Write clear input references, error handling, and timeouts for each node. 3. Use Test node with mock upstream input to validate a single node first. The current Loop is saved before testing. 4. Click Run once and check each node's input, output, timing, and errors in the Run log , Run history , and Audit report . 5. After validation, turn on Enabled , enable AI-callable as needed, configure schedules or webhooks, and keep human approvals before key steps. Figure 1: The Create Loop canvas connects multiple processing nodes into a runnable flow. Select a node to inspect its parameters on the right. Inputs, outputs, and permissions - Reads: workspace files, upstream node output, Loop definitions, run history, and approval status. - Writes: Loop definitions are stored in local domain state; nodes can write to the workspace; each run saves a run Manifest and per-node receipts and provides an audit report. - Approval or external effects: starting an entire flow, stopping a run, and handling approvals are governed as external writes and require confirmation. HTTP and AI nodes make real requests and incur costs. - What it does not do: write raw Secret values to run records, restore paused approvals after the app restarts, or approve on a person's behalf. Known limitations - Human approval pause state is held in memory, and an app restart loses that run. Important flows should make nodes repeatable and keep idempotency keys. - Schedules and webhooks depend on the app process. They do not fire while the app is closed. - Secret variables store only the slot and fingerprint. When a Secret is required and no safe replay resolution is available, execution blocks rather than continuing with an empty value. - A single-node test proves only that node, not the whole flow. Tests also execute the node logic for real. - When randomness is not fixed, rerun differences are marked as indeterminate and cannot be treated directly as a reproduction failure. Related pages - Automation and scheduled tasks: scheduled execution of a single AI instruction, and when to use Create Loop instead. - Evidence & Reproducibility: run records, artifact versions, and the evidence chain. - Agent workflows: Agent hooks and execution boundaries in sessions. - Permissions and security: external requests, writes, and confirmation rules. Implementation basis: @sciforge/domain-create-loop v1.1.4.

en.title: Dataset API
en.description: Migration note for the retired Dataset API, and how to record where your data came from.
en.body: Dataset API In the current source baseline, the old dataset-api domain is retired. The built-in API described in earlier versions of this page is no longer provided. This page keeps its original URL so old links and historical records can still find it. The old data-source catalog, UI-registered endpoints, S3 object browsing, preparation plans, checkpoint recovery, and validate-and-publish flow are no longer available operations. Do not assume old .sciforge/datasets records were migrated automatically or can still be executed. Keep the original files and source material, and check them one by one. To obtain data, use the data provider's supported client, or your own scripts and environment. Record the source URL, access time, data version, license, download parameters, file size, and SHA-256. Manage credentials as described in Permissions & security. The old page's rule that retries had to go through the Dataset API does not apply to a retired capability. Supported downloaded files can be viewed in Life Science Preview, and Biology Room can organize the sequence, structure, and genome assets it supports. Data acquisition, cleaning, and scientific conclusions still each need real execution and source records; see Evidence & reproducibility. These two built-in biology features do not replace the old Dataset API's data ingestion and publishing service.

en.title: Evidence & Reproducibility
en.description: Use artifact versions, Checkpoints, Evidence DAG, and Research Dossier to pin down the research process and its results.
en.body: Evidence & Reproducibility After a research task is complete, a summary that looks correct is not the same as a reproducible deliverable. SciForge uses several complementary objects to record "what happened, what was produced, what it was based on, and where to continue next time." These records come from built-in features and optional plugins together, so not all seven pages in this group describe standalone plugins. The current breakdown is below; for versions, see Version & Compatibility: Recording feature Purpose and availability --- --- Artifact Versions Built in; records immutable versions of a single artifact, comparison, and restore Git Checkpoints Built-in feature; a separate plugin still awaiting full integration pins the Git state at a given stage Research Checkpoints Built-in feature; a separate plugin still awaiting full integration saves research-stage context and the resume location Change Inspector Standalone production plugin; reads file changes in the current session Evidence DAG Built-in claim and evidence relationships; an optional backend plugin is not yet integrated into the app Project DAG Built-in project-level goals and review records; a backend plugin artifact is still awaiting app integration Research Dossier Built in; organizes research deliverables for other people Choose the right record object Object Problem it solves Typical content --- --- --- Session How did the task progress? Messages, tool calls, commands, approvals, and the final response Artifact Version How did a chart or file change over time? Artifact path, version, inputs, and generation details Git Checkpoint What stage are the workspace files at? Git status and stage-level code snapshots Research Checkpoint How do I resume a research stage? Research context, key artifacts, and resume location Evidence DAG What supports or refutes a claim? Claims, sources, methods, artifacts, limitations, and relationships Research Dossier How does someone else read the final deliverable? Research question, inputs, methods, results, credibility, and limitations Build an auditable chain Recommended order: 1. At the start of the task, record the workspace, input versions, and objective. 2. After key computations, save the commands, parameters, and artifacts. 3. Create artifact versions for charts or reports. 4. Connect key claims to inputs, methods, and charts. 5. Manually check counterevidence, missing data, and inference boundaries. 6. Save a Checkpoint and generate a Research Dossier. Figure 1: The research dossier shows the research narrative, current version, credibility summary, and limitations that need attention. Have the agent leave a complete record You can add the following to a task: After completing the analysis, put the research question, input files, methods used, key parameters, results, and limitations into the research dossier. Every key conclusion should trace back to its source, derived table, or figure; mark anything you cannot confirm as unverified. Do not just ask for "generate an Evidence DAG." First clarify which claims are worth reviewing, which data can directly support them, and which interpretations are still candidate hypotheses. Manual review checklist - Can every key number be traced back to an input file and a computation step? - Do the charts come from verified derived tables rather than hand-edited intermediate files? - Does the conclusion confuse correlation, prediction, and causation? - Are counterevidence, warnings, and missing data still visible? - Are the code commit, environment, parameters, and random seed needed to rerun all present? - Does the Checkpoint correspond to a Git state that has been verified? Before you use these features First confirm that the feature is available in the current app; optional plugins also require installation, activation, and a license for the corresponding version. A package in the source, passing tests, or a generated installer does not mean it has been published in the public marketplace. The current seven standalone plugins and their licenses are listed in Plugin licenses. Optional Evidence DAG 1.0.0 currently verifies the backend slice only; host cross-process integration has not been delivered, so it cannot be used as a complete app plugin. Built-in Evidence still handles evidence recording for current figure acceptance; do not let the built-in feature and the optional plugin write to the same evidence directory at the same time. Synthetic data in tests and local samples do not represent real research conclusions or marketplace release acceptance. Scientific Figures independently saves code, inputs, environment, runs, and figure history, and does not automatically register with Artifact Versions or Evidence DAG. When including figures in a deliverable, explicitly link the actual inputs, runs, and outputs, and re-verify them before forming claims. Data boundaries Evidence DAG and Research Dossier show meaningful content only when the current workspace and session already contain the corresponding data. An empty panel does not indicate a malfunction; first have the task generate explicit claims, sources, and artifact records. Case: ECCITE-seq cross-scale virtual cell evidence atlas.

en.title: Evidence DAG
en.description: Connect claims in a session to their sources, methods, artifacts, and limitations.
en.body: Evidence DAG Evidence DAG helps you check what a conclusion rests on: in the graph, see the sources, computation steps, figures, and limitations that support or refute it. After you finish an analysis, click Update to save the evidence relationships as they stand at that point. To combine several sessions, use Project DAG. How to open it - Entry: in the Research panel, click View evidence graph . When the standalone evidence panel is open, switch from the default Research record to Evidence graph . - Target: committed evidence snapshots in the current Runtime and session. - Prerequisite: the task has produced a compilable trace, and the Evidence service and text-reasoning configuration are available. What you can do What you want to do How to do it Output --- --- --- Leave a reviewable trace Keep sources, computation records, and artifact references during analysis Runtime trace increments Generate a new snapshot Click Update and wait for queueing and commit to finish An immutable Evidence snapshot Inspect claims and evidence Select a node in the graph to view its sources, runs, artifacts, and relationships The in-session evidence graph Check provenance breakpoints Review provenance coverage, breakpoints, and limitation notes A list of evidence gaps Run a structure audit Click Audit to run a read-only check against the committed snapshot L0 audit results Download a rerun spec Select a Conclusion node and click Download rerun spec A .sciforge-rerun.json file Typical workflow 1. Complete a round of analysis and confirm that key conclusions have sources, computation records, and matching artifacts. 2. Click Update and confirm the status moves from queued to running and then to committed. 3. Check the full chain from claim to source, run, code, environment, and artifact version. 4. Go through the prompts about a missing source, an unverified version, or a missing approval one by one; add the real records, then update. 5. When you need a cross-session, project-level view, move on to the Project DAG. Inputs, outputs, and permissions - Reads: runtime traces visible to the current session, tool receipts, committed snapshots, Artifact versions, and source anchors. - Writes: evidence delta storage, immutable snapshots, and the audit sidecar; rerun specs are exported from committed snapshots. - Approval or external effects: updating needs no extra approval, but it writes evidence state and snapshots and calls the configured text-reasoning service; downloading a rerun spec is read-only. Rebuilding is an advanced operation and requires specifying a reason and writing a justification. - What it does not do: promote chat summaries or raw tool receipts directly to scientific artifacts, infer missing metadata from prose, or rewrite committed snapshots. Known limitations - The graph may be empty if the task has not yet saved claims, sources, or artifact records; check the records first, then update. - Only nodes and edges in committed snapshots are audit-eligible; pending failures are shown separately and never make the committed graph unusable. - Promoting a claim to L4 requires a stable run record, verifiable inputs, exact software, parameters, environment, and logs or artifacts; stochastic runs must also supply a random seed. - Missing fields become named provenance breakpoints and are never filled in by inference; the built-in audit currently performs deterministic L0 structural checks. - Rebuilding is only for schema upgrades, corruption recovery, or reinterpretation, not a routine editing entry point; previews of restricted evidence fail according to the access policy. Related pages - Evidence & Reproducibility: the group overview and the recommended record chain. - Project DAG: aggregate the committed snapshots of several sessions into a project view. - Research Dossier: the reading-oriented delivery surface. - Artifact Versions: the immutable artifact versions that evidence references. - Virtual cell evidence atlas case: how evidence is organized in a complete task. Implementation basis: @sciforge/domain-evidence-dag v2.13.0.

en.title: Skills, MCP, and Extensions
en.description: See where capabilities come from in the Extension Center, manage extensions and Skills, and check MCP and desktop-control permissions.
en.body: Skills, MCP, and Extensions When you need to add tools or a specialized method, first work out what you are installing, then check its source and permissions. Extensions provide app panels and tools, Skills provide task methods, and MCP connects external tools or data. This page reflects the implementation as of 2026-11-06. For installed versions and available capabilities, see Version & Compatibility. Open the Extension Center Open Extensions from the left sidebar to see built-in and installed extensions, the marketplace, and Skills. Expand the sidebar first if you need the full navigation. Extension details show the publisher, version, source, status, permissions, and the features it contributes. After installing or enabling, related entries may appear in the left navigation, the vertical toolbar on the far right, or file preview. When there are many toolbar entries, use More tools ; supported entries can be adjusted through Customize toolbar . Old interface: for understanding extension sources and feature details; the current layout follows the body text. Install and manage extensions In the marketplace, pick an entry and read the description, publisher, permissions, and installation status before confirming the install. Whether it can be installed depends on the current index and app compatibility; a blocked entry shows the reason. Ordinary local installation uses an official signed package, and checks the signature, file contents, and Host API compatibility. Development sources are labeled separately and must not be treated as official signed installs. Files in a workspace never become enabled extensions automatically. Installed extensions can be enabled, disabled, uninstalled, or rolled back with the operations the interface offers; built-in extensions are managed with the app version. If it says a restart is needed, or the extension is invalid or failed to load, handle that prompt first, then check the feature's entry point. Extension pages that support docking can be placed on the left, right, bottom, or in the main area, and used together with the session. Changing position does not widen the extension's permissions. Use a Skill A Skill usually contains method notes plus supporting scripts and material. Before enabling it, check: - What tasks it suits, and when it triggers. - Whether it runs scripts, accesses the network, or writes files. - What software, data, and credentials it needs. - What check shows the result is reliable. Old interface: shows what project-level and global Skill management is for. Once a Skill is discovered, its scripts still run under the task's permissions. Dependency installs and external actions of a third-party Skill need separate checks; "enabled" is not a substitute for authorization. Connect an MCP Server When configuring MCP, check the service source, version, launch method or address, the credential scope, and what data the tools will read or send. Test the connection with low-impact operations first, then move to tasks that write. Before sending, uploading, deleting, or modifying anything in an external system, confirm the target and the user's authorization. A successful connection only shows that the service can be called; the task result still needs checking. Avoid writing keys directly into prompts, project requirements, or delivery content. Use Computer Use Desktop control needs Runtime support, an available backend, and system permissions. Check the backend status in settings; on macOS, also check the Screen Recording and Accessibility permissions. Limit the target app and the task scope, and check each action such as sign-in, authorization, payment, sending, or deleting. Old interface: shows that the Runtime, Backend, and system permissions each need checking. When you cannot find a feature 1. Check the status and error messages of the extension, Skill, or MCP. 2. Check whether the current workspace, permissions, and Runtime support the capability you need. 3. Start a new session so capabilities are discovered again; if a restart is needed, follow the interface prompt. 4. If a tool entry has disappeared, check More tools and the toolbar customization settings. 5. If a local extension fails to install, check the publisher, signature, and version compatibility; do not force-load it by turning off permission checks. Related pages: Workbench tools, Permissions & security.

en.title: Git Checkpoints
en.description: Pin Git state at task-turn boundaries and automatically leave a rescue snapshot before restoring.
en.body: Git Checkpoints Git Checkpoints record Git snapshots of the workspace before and after task turns, pinning down "what state the code was in before this turn started and after it finished." It owns only checkpoint metadata and restore policy; actual repository operations run through the generic version control capability. Research context itself is recorded by Research Checkpoints. How to open it - Entry: Git Checkpoints in the right toolbar (expand More tools if it is not visible); the right panel is also titled Git Checkpoints . - Scope: the local Git workspace bound to the current session. - Prerequisite: the workspace is a Git repository and a version control provider is available; non-Git workspaces do not produce checkpoints. What you can do What you want to do How to do it Output --- --- --- View turn checkpoints Open the panel and view records before and after turns in chronological order A checkpoint list and stages Review the scope of changes Select a checkpoint and view the workspace patch and change summary A diff preview Restore a known state Select the target checkpoint, click Restore , and confirm A workspace back at that snapshot Avoid losing state during restore No extra action is needed; the system captures it automatically before restoring A rescue checkpoint ID Refresh the current list Click the refresh icon to reload The latest checkpoint list Typical workflow 1. Start a task in a Git workspace; the system records a pre-turn checkpoint. 2. After the turn completes or ends, refresh the panel and confirm that a post-turn checkpoint appears. 3. Select the target checkpoint, review the patch preview first, and then decide whether to restore. 4. To restore, click Restore and confirm, then wait for the system to create a rescue checkpoint first. 5. After the restore completes, re-check the workspace state and have Change Inspector inspect the file changes in the current session. Inputs, outputs, and permissions - Reads: workspace Git state, snapshot metadata, patches, and change summaries. - Writes: checkpoint metadata is written to the app data directory; restoring rewrites workspace files. - Approval or external effects: restoring is destructive and requires explicit confirmation; if rescue checkpoint creation fails, the restore is aborted. - What it does not do: run Git commands directly or bypass version control provider policy, or fabricate checkpoints in non-Git workspaces. Known limitations - The current implementation covers turn-boundary checkpoints in local Git workspaces; the panel provides listing, preview, refresh, and restore. - The panel has no button for creating checkpoints manually; checkpoints are triggered by the turn lifecycle and do not depend on the panel staying open or on a manual save. - A version control provider may truncate the patch preview, in which case only part of the diff is visible. - Restoring is a workspace-level rollback, not a read-only comparison; the rescue checkpoint is a protection point captured automatically before the restore. - It does not store research questions, sources, or resume locations, so it cannot replace a Research Checkpoint. Related pages - Evidence & Reproducibility: the group overview and the recommended record chain. - Research Checkpoints: save research context and the resume location. - Artifact Versions: pin a single artifact instead of the whole workspace. - Change Inspector: check which files a session actually changed. - Workspaces and sessions: how workspaces, sessions, and Git state relate. Implementation basis: @sciforge/domain-git-checkpoints v1.0.3.

en.title: Identity & Access
en.description: Manage the local account, cloud sign-in, device connection, and usage summary from the bottom of the sidebar.
en.body: Identity & Access Expand the workbench's left sidebar and look at the bottom for the local account, cloud status, and usage summary . Click the account row to open the account panel; click the cloud row to open the same panel positioned at SciForge Cloud . Settings sits below it. This page reflects the implementation as of 2026-11-06. For differences between the installed version and the public source, see Version & Compatibility. A local account is an attribution marker Local features do not require sign-in. You can create a local account, confirm its display name, choose an account or rename it, and sign out of the account. A local account provides no security authentication and does not isolate workspaces, chats, settings, API keys, or tool data . On a shared computer, switching the display name is no substitute for operating-system account isolation. The delete button on an account row first shows a confirmation area. Once confirmed, it deletes that local account and its attribution data on this machine, and this cannot be undone. When you delete the current account, the system selects the earliest-created remaining account; after the last account is deleted, no account is selected. Delete account here is local identity management. It is not cloud account cancellation, project deletion, or workspace file cleanup. Signing out of a local account, signing out of the cloud, and disconnecting a device each do something different, so check the button name and its target before acting. Sign in to the cloud and connect a device 1. Create or choose a local account first. Until one is selected, "Browser sign-in" is unavailable. 2. Under SciForge Cloud , click Browser sign-in and complete authentication in the system browser. You do not need to paste a password or token into a session. 3. After returning, check the cloud identity. If no device is connected yet, click Connect this device . 4. Collaboration features that depend on cloud identity can continue only when the identity is valid and the device is active. The local account, the model provider sign-in, and the SciForge cloud sign-in are separate configurations. Cloud features depend on the current app configuration and service availability; they do not require you to set up any old collection of domain packages first. Panel state or action Meaning and what to do --- --- Not signed in to the cloud Local features still work; cloud projects need sign-in This device is not connected Being signed in is not a device connection; connect the device from the interface Connecting this device Wait for the device registration result and avoid repeating the action This device is connected The device is active; a valid cloud identity and project permission are still required This device is disconnected / connection error Cloud permissions cannot be used as if connected normally; check the error and recover as prompted Sign in again Completes cloud authentication again; it does not automatically accept project invitations or tasks Sign out Clears the current cloud sign-in session; do not treat it as having revoked the device registration Disconnect this device Revokes this device's cloud access; local features are kept When a device is revoked, the identity changes, or device validity cannot be confirmed, cloud authentication rights are withdrawn. Do not use a cached display name to decide you are still authorized. If sign-in or connection fails, retry as the panel suggests and keep the original task and drafts. Reading the usage summary The bottom of the sidebar shows token and cost summaries for today and the last 7 days , read from the daily usage the Runtime has recorded. It is not a cloud account balance or a provider bill, and switching local accounts does not prove the usage data is isolated. Loading, no data, and load failure each show their own message. No data does not mean no model requests were made. Cost depends on the metering and pricing information available; settlement is still governed by the provider's own records. Credentials and recovery boundaries Cloud sign-in material and device keys are managed by the platform's secure storage. When secure storage is unavailable, do not fall back to plaintext files or put credentials into chats, requirements, or delivery files. When the local identity database is unavailable, other local features still work. The recovery entry asks you to type a confirmation text, first creates and verifies a backup, and then resets the local identity data. It is not a reset tool for the whole app's data. Related pages: Collaboration, Runtime & models, Permissions & security.

en.title: Life Science Preview
en.description: View structure, sequence, omics, imaging, and spectral files directly in the workspace.
en.body: Life Science Preview Life Science Preview is a preview submodule of the built-in @sciforge/domain-biology-workbench 1.1.3 . It shares one domain package with Biology Room, ships with the app, and needs no marketplace install or plugin enablement. It routes common scientific files to 6 preview slots and 5 kinds of viewer; the companion-index slot only transports. The old standalone life-science-preview plugin and domain package have been removed, while the preview slots and wire identifiers stay compatible. For how versions are quoted, see Version & Compatibility. Opening it - Entry point: file preview in the file panel; open a supported local or remote workspace file. - Applies to: workspace files. The view is chosen from the extension and the preview manifest. - Prerequisite: the file is in the current workspace. For a remote workspace, the remote Workspace Host reads it, and the interface does not require downloading the whole file to this machine first. What it can do What you want to do How Output --- --- --- View molecular structures Open .pdb , .cif , .mmcif , .sdf , .mol , .mol2 , .xyz Chain, residue, and ligand summary; Mol view; distance, angle, or dihedral measurement when coordinates are available View sequences and genomes Open .fasta , .fa , .fna , .faa , .fastq , .gb , .gbk , .gff , .gff3 , .gtf , .bed , .vcf Record count, length, features, intervals, variant summary, and region selection View omics matrices Open .h5ad , .loom , .mtx , .h5 , .hdf5 , .zarr Matrix dimensions, observation/variable keys, embedding names, and a metadata summary View biological imaging Open .tif , .tiff , .ome.tif , .ome.tiff , .czi , .svs , .ndpi Size, channels, OME metadata, region of interest (ROI) and channel selection; thumbnails and tiles for TIFF/OME-TIFF View spectra and proteomics Open .mzml , .mzxml , .mgf , .fcs Scan/event summary, peak count, intensity range, sampled peaks, and peak-interval annotations Carry a companion index Open .fai , .gzi , .tbi , .csi Transported as the companion index of a sequence or genome file, for later object references What is not parsed: For omics, only metadata is read; HDF5, AnnData, Loom, and Zarr matrices are not decoded. CZI, SVS, and NDPI give only container-metadata placeholders and no pixel decoding. FCS mainly shows the visible header, keywords, and a sampled-peak summary, without a full event matrix. Trajectory and density files can be handed to the Mol view, but they are outside the scope of chain, residue, and ligand summaries. The preview is a reading aid, not validation-grade format parsing or an analysis tool. Molecular selection and what gets saved A molecular selection can express multiple chains, residues, atoms, and ligands. The Inspector offers chain, ligand, and clear actions. A selection sent back by the host is synced to Mol , including the latest selection during asynchronous initialization. The source file stays read-only. After changes, reopen the file and check the selection. For now there is no commitment that every click in the 3D viewport is saved automatically, or that rapid successive selections are kept in order. A highlight in the viewport does not by itself mean the selection was saved. Typical workflow 1. Confirm the workspace location at the top, and open the target file in the file panel. 2. Check the format, size, dimensions, or record count in the preview to make sure you opened the right file. 3. To continue the analysis, create a region, residue, or channel selection and let the agent work on the original file. 4. In a remote workspace, first confirm that reading happens on the remote side. Do not have the agent copy a whole large file just for the preview. 5. Treat preview results only as session context. Key conclusions should still go back to the original file and the computation records. Inputs, outputs, and permissions - Reads: preview summaries read the beginning of the file, up to 2,000,000 bytes of text and 4 MiB of binary. Anything beyond that is marked as truncated, and the Workspace Host that owns the data does the reading. - Writes: the preview itself does not modify the source file. Export only copies the source file, in the same format, to a new workspace path. - Approval or external effects: opening and reading need no approval. Exporting a copy needs confirmation and writes to a new workspace path. - What it does not do: it does not convert formats, repair damaged files, treat a preview summary as complete data, or upload workspace files. Known limitations - Observation lists are truncated with an explicit marker, and selections that are too large are rejected. - Omics matrices, proprietary imaging containers, and FCS get metadata or placeholder previews only, so do not use them for quantitative analysis. - Thumbnails and tiles for biological imaging are attempted only for TIFF/OME-TIFF; compressed or non-8-bit TIFFs may fall back to metadata. - Sequence and genome previews are based on truncated text and cannot replace full format validation or variant calling. - Unregistered extensions do not enter the dedicated views above and are still handled as ordinary workspace files. Related pages - Biology Room: organize multiple sequences, structures, and annotations into a traceable room. - Dataset API migration note: the old data-ingestion service is retired; obtain data through the provider's client or your own environment and keep the source records. - Workbench tools: how files, the terminal, the browser, and other entry points divide the work. - Feature status & limits: see the current position on each capability. Current version: built-in Biology Workbench 1.1.3. Preview reads and file transfer are still subject to workspace permissions and size limits.

en.title: Features & Extensions overview
en.description: Choose workbench, research analysis, evidence, collaboration, and extension capabilities by the task you want to do.
en.body: Features & Extensions overview Pick the task you want to do from the table below. Built-in features open directly; standalone plugins must be installed; Skills provide working methods; MCP connects external tools. For version information, see Version & Compatibility. Start from your task What you want to do Where to read Current form and conditions --- --- --- Open a project, continue a session, view or edit files Workbench Local workspace, sessions, and file preview for supported formats. Files cannot be edited directly when they are truncated, read-only, or have no write-back channel. Connect models and executors Runtime & models Codex, Claude Code, and DSH are configured separately. Model access and tool permissions are not the same thing. View sequences, structures, omics, imaging, and spectra Life Science Preview A preview submodule of the built-in Biology Workbench. Organize biological objects and experiment records Biology Room Another role of the same Biology Workbench package, not an extra marketplace plugin. Plot from data and code, revise, and accept candidates Scientific Figures Standalone plugin. Needs a compatible host, Python, and the required dependencies. Add anchored comments to text or resources Anchored Comments Standalone plugin. Real capture and external feedback each have their own permission requirements. Check what the agent actually changed Change Inspector Plugin you must install. Lets the agent list this session's file differences, and tells you when output is too long. Save artifacts and research evidence Evidence & reproducibility Saves file versions, research stages, and the source of conclusions. Figure records must be linked separately. Run repeated tasks Automation, Create Loop Needs the app running and the matching executor. Multi-step flows and single scheduled instructions are configured separately. Sign in, connect a device, join a project, and deliver tasks Account, Collaboration Local accounts and cloud identity are separate. Team actions also need an available service and role authorization. Use Content Space and notes Content Space, SiYuan Notes You configure the matching service. Server deployment tutorials are not included. Add plugins, working methods, or external tools Extensions & marketplace Compatible signed packages, Skills, and MCP are each configured separately. An empty marketplace does not mean built-in features were uninstalled. Evidence and tool reference - Artifact Versions, Git Checkpoints, Research Checkpoints: fix the state of files or research stages. - Evidence DAG, Project DAG, Research Dossier: organize evidence, project goals, and deliverables. - Terminal, Browser Preview, Computer Use: use external execution capabilities according to the runtime environment and permissions. - Plugin license terms: check licenses, host dependencies, and the current installation boundary. Migrations and retirements Dataset API and Scientific Compute have left the current product line. Their old addresses keep a data-acquisition migration note and a compute migration note. The old Visual Review is also no longer listed as a standalone installable plugin. Do not restore removed entry points or install old directories based on old screenshots. Historical material on Paper Radar and OpenContent does not represent current capabilities. Remote SSH connection and management belong to internal supplements, and the public manual does not provide VPN, SSH target registration, or internal deployment steps. The local mock Provider is for development and testing only. How to tell whether you can use something Check the current client version, plugin source, and host dependencies first, then see Feature status. A page describing an implementation does not mean every platform has a release package. Historical screenshots and cases keep their own date, platform, and acceptance version. This round did not re-run GUI verification for every feature; source checks and actual acceptance are recorded separately.

en.title: Project DAG
en.description: Aggregate project goals, claims, review status, and decisions across sessions.
en.body: Project DAG Project DAG combines the evidence from several sessions in the same project, to help you see which conclusions the project has so far and which questions still need review. First save evidence in each session's Evidence DAG, then set a goal here, update the project graph, and trace sources. How to open it - Entry: the Project DAG panel on the right; resource navigation from a project, Goal, or Snapshot opens the corresponding view. - Target: the project that corresponds to the current workspace, along with its committed Evidence snapshots. - Prerequisite: the project has at least one committed Evidence snapshot, and both the Evidence and Project services are available. What you can do What you want to do How to do it Output --- --- --- View the project-wide graph Open the panel and read the latest committed Project snapshot Project-level claims, findings, and review status Set a project goal Fill in the title and description under Project goal and click Save goal A new Goal version Aggregate new evidence Click Update now and wait for the task to commit A new Project snapshot and receipt See what needs attention Review the attention count, audit status, and review package A to-do list Return to session evidence Click Open Evidence DAG for session The evidence graph of that session View claim provenance Select a Claim to see the strongest provenance path, sources, L0–L4, and breakpoints Cross-layer provenance details and related decisions Typical workflow 1. Complete analyses in several sessions and commit a snapshot in the Evidence DAG for each. 2. Open the Project DAG, fill in the project goal, and save it. 3. Click Update now and confirm that the receipt moves through queued and running to committed. 4. Review the attention items and key Claims, jumping back to the source session to verify when needed. 5. For restricted sources, read only the redacted paths and breakpoints; do not try to bypass the access policy. Inputs, outputs, and permissions - Reads: committed Evidence snapshots, project graphs, Claims, audit records, and decision records. - Writes: project update tasks, Goal versions, and immutable Project snapshots; audits write only to a separate sidecar. - Approval or external effects: panel operations are limited to local project records; any publication or external delivery still requires Runtime authorization, which project policy cannot replace. - What it does not do: read raw chat, accept uncommitted source graphs, modify the graph directly from the audit page, or cache the content of Evidence snapshots. Known limitations - The current implementation consumes only committed Evidence snapshots; an upstream commit merely marks the project as needing a refresh and does not compile each item automatically. - When the Project view is closed, nothing is precompiled; to get a new view, update explicitly and wait for the persistence receipt. - After a new snapshot is committed, audits that are queued, running, completed, or failed on the old snapshot are marked stale, and old Findings never overwrite the new graph. - Sources you are not allowed to view have their content hidden, and only limited status and gap hints are shown. - The audit checks an existing project graph; an audit failure does not undo a graph that was already saved, and it does not modify conclusions directly. Related pages - Evidence & Reproducibility: the group overview and the recommended record chain. - Evidence DAG: the only evidence source for the project graph. - Research Dossier: turn project results into an external deliverable. - Workspaces and sessions: how several sessions share one project scope. - Permissions and security: the boundary between access policy and publication authorization. Implementation basis: @sciforge/domain-project-dag v1.0.9.

en.title: Research Checkpoints
en.description: Automatically turn each round of research conversation into a recoverable, immutable checkpoint.
en.body: Research Checkpoints Research Checkpoints automatically records accepted and completed chat turns as immutable research checkpoints. It saves the research summary, reason for changes, sources, files, and Git references for that round, and flags operations that are not yet tracked. It answers "where do I continue next time, and what was the basis at the time?" It stores research context and a resume location, not the workspace snapshots recorded by Git Checkpoints; artifact bytes and version identity are stored by Artifact Versions. How to open it - Entry: Research record for this turn on the session result card; the card offers Open research dossier . - Scope: completed chat turns in the current Runtime and session. - Prerequisite: automatic recording is on by default, the session is bound to a workspace, and v1 is generated after the first turn completes. What you can do What you want to do How to do it Output --- --- --- Record each research turn automatically Complete a research chat as usual and wait for the record to be saved An immutable checkpoint version View this turn's record View the title, reason for changes, inputs, and outputs on the result card A research summary for this turn Open an exact output Select an output under Exact artifact versions and click Open The corresponding artifact version Go to the full dossier Click Open research dossier The exact record in the research dossier Handle a version conflict Save again based on the current version, or discard this turn's record A conflict-resolution receipt Start or stop recording Use Start automatic recording / Stop automatic recording in the research dossier A new policy revision number Typical workflow 1. Open a session with a workspace and confirm that research recording is on automatically. 2. Complete a research turn and wait for the result card to show that the record has been saved. 3. Check the status of inputs, outputs, reproducibility, provenance, controls, and evidence. 4. Review untracked operations and add the actual commands, environment, and outputs for later review. 5. To continue, select a historical record in the research dossier and restore it as a new version. Inputs, outputs, and permissions - Reads: turn content, tool receipts, workspace file changes, artifacts, compute runs, and Git references. - Writes: checkpoint manifests and record bindings are committed as new versions; artifact bytes are still stored by Artifact Versions. - Approval or external effects: importing an old session, resolving a conflict, and restoring as a new version require confirmation; starting or stopping recording returns a new policy revision number. - What it does not do: silently backfill conversations from periods when recording was stopped, promote Terminal, IDE, or PTY activity to controlled execution, or rewrite existing versions. Known limitations - The current implementation covers only accepted and completed chat turns; turns during periods when recording is stopped are not backfilled. - Ordinary Terminal, exec_command , IDE, file watchers, Git diff, and post-hoc hashes count only as observations; the related output remains untracked or incomplete. - Importing an old session preserves chat content only; the record is permanently marked legacy / incomplete and carries blocking provenance breakpoints. - New checkpoints are visible only within the workspace and cannot be exported by default; query parameters that resemble narrative, URLs, or credentials are redacted, but this is not a general content-leak prevention system. - When record ownership cannot be confirmed temporarily, the record is shown as pending and is not automatically assigned to a turn. Related pages - Evidence & Reproducibility: the group overview and the recommended record chain. - Research Dossier: view records, control automatic recording, and restore historical versions. - Git Checkpoints: save a workspace Git snapshot rather than research context. - Artifact Versions: store the artifact bytes and versions that a checkpoint references. - Workspaces and sessions: how a session scopes recording. Implementation basis: @sciforge/domain-research-checkpoints v1.0.5.

en.title: Research Dossier
en.description: Turn the research question, inputs, methods, results, and limitations into a readable deliverable.
en.body: Research Dossier The research dossier puts the research summary, sources, key artifacts, versions, and limitations together, for review and delivery. After opening a research record, read the results and the limitations that need attention first, then expand versions and technical details as needed. Process records come from Research Checkpoints, and evidence relationships are in Evidence DAG. How to open it - Entry: Research in the right toolbar (expand More tools if it is not shown); the right panel is titled Research as well; Open research dossier on a session result card binds to the exact version. - By default it shows the current research stage. To see history, open a specific artifact version or research record. References to the old Scientific Compute may still appear, but that compute service has been retired. - Prerequisite: the session is bound to a workspace. Once there are research checkpoints or artifact versions, you can view the detailed records. The research dossier brings the research narrative, version position, trust summary, and the limitations to consider onto one reading surface. What you can do What you want to do How to do it Output --- --- --- Read a research record Open it from an exact version or a compute run Overview, key artifacts, and trust summary Inspect research limitations Review Limitations to consider and Breakpoints An actionable list of limitations Browse historical versions Load older versions in the Versions area The version list and the current position Compare or restore Use Compare exact version or Restore as new version A diff summary and a new current version Preview or export Use Open verified preview or Export Bundle V2 A verified preview and a portable bundle Manage automatic recording Start or stop automatic recording, or import earlier chats A policy revision number and legacy records Typical workflow 1. Complete a round of research and click Open research dossier on the result card. 2. Check the exact target and version position, expanding technical details when needed to view the Version ID and digest. 3. Read the overview, research sources, declared files, reproduction status, and limitations. 4. To trace back or roll back, compare exact versions or restore as a new version, and check the receipt from the owning domain. 5. Before delivery, export Bundle V2 and confirm that access restrictions and unverified items are clearly accounted for. Inputs, outputs, and permissions - Reads: exact records from owning domains such as artifact versions, research checkpoints, compute runs, evidence, and Git checkpoints. - Writes: the dossier itself writes no records; restore, import, and the recording switch are all delegated to the owning domain. - Approval or external effects: restore and legacy-session import follow the confirmation policy of the owning domain; exporting a Bundle writes workspace files and asks for confirmation. - What it does not do: keep a copy of records, own the current pointer, or fall back to latest when a record is missing or a digest does not match. Known limitations - What you see depends on the checkpoints, artifact versions, and evidence the task has saved. If there are no records yet, finish and save a round of the task first. - The dossier itself stores no records; when an owning domain is unavailable, only the corresponding block degrades, and the rest of the verified content remains readable. - If the requested version is missing or fails verification, an error is shown; another version is never opened quietly. - Imported legacy sessions are permanently marked legacy / incomplete and keep a blocking provenance breakpoint. - Empty blocks and inapplicable compute, evidence, or review blocks are omitted; return to the Evidence DAG when you need the full relationship graph. Related pages - Evidence & Reproducibility: the group overview and the recommended record chain. - Research Checkpoints: the upstream source of the records and restore actions in the dossier. - Artifact Versions: the exact version source that the dossier opens and compares. - Evidence DAG: the complete in-session evidence relationships behind the dossier. - Feature status and limitations: how the Partially available status is judged. Implementation basis: @sciforge/domain-research-dossier v1.6.0.

en.title: Scientific Compute
en.description: Migration note for the retired capability, and how to keep records of real computation.
en.body: Scientific Compute In the current source baseline, the old scientific-compute domain is retired. It no longer provides a callable built-in capability or a standalone plugin. This page keeps its original URL so old links and historical records can still find it. The old page described a local, deterministic fixture job loop used to test the event trail of submission, monitoring, blocking, and recovery. It never represented real cluster scheduling or real scientific results. Do not keep looking for the status query, the four-scenario baseline run, or the job-monitoring entry point it described. For real computation, use the workbench terminal and your own compute environment. For remote files and where execution happens, see Remote & collaboration. Keep the actual commands, an input summary, software versions, parameters, exit status, and output files, and organize them as described in Evidence & reproducibility. Python + Matplotlib figures can use the standalone Scientific Figures plugin. Its code and input snapshots and run receipts are not a general job scheduler. The current baseline should not be read as a promise of built-in Slurm, PBS, or Kubernetes scheduling.

en.title: Scientific Figures
en.description: Select files, describe the plot you want in chat, really run Python, and compare and accept candidate figures.
en.body: Scientific Figures Select files → tell the AI how to draw → review the result → accept when satisfied. Scientific Figures ties a text request, Python code, an actual run, and image versions together. To revise an image, just keep typing the change; you do not need to box, arrow, or pin anything on the image. The current source is @sciforge/plugin-scientific-plotting 0.4.0-mvp.11 , which supports the native DSH panel and the SciForge adapter entry. The 2026-11-05 case and screenshots kept in this page come from 0.4.0-mvp.10 and from earlier versions where explicitly marked; they have not been re-accepted as mvp.11. The accepted environment is macOS arm64, the DSH Runtime, and Python + Matplotlib. For public marketplace availability, see the actual release record, and for the compatibility baseline see Version & Compatibility. R/MATLAB execution is not implemented yet. For the actual steps and screenshots of multi-file cleaning, four-panel figures, missing-value matrices, and failure recovery, see Complex scientific figure case. Installing and opening 1. In Extensions → Marketplace , find the Scientific Figures package compatible with your SciForge version, check the publisher and permissions, approve the installation, and enable it. If it is not listed, the maintainer must supply a signed package and its installation source. 2. Open a writable local workspace and a DSH session whose model is configured. 3. In SciForge, select Scientific Figures from the plugin picker in the right sidebar. In native DSH, use the Figures panel in the session input area, or type /scientific-figures . The default Figure page contains file input, text input, and image preview. The machine needs a working Python and Matplotlib. In the plugin configuration, point pythonCommand to an interpreter you have confirmed works; the default python3 does not mean Matplotlib is installed. The plugin does not install dependencies automatically. Before running, you can ask the Agent to query status to check the configuration; a successful configuration check still needs an actual run to confirm the environment works. Native DSH requires =0.2.1-rc.4 <0.3.0 and Node =22. The SciForge adapter entry currently runs only on macOS environments that pass the isolation check; installing the plugin successfully does not remove the execution limits on Windows and Linux. The package contains the native Canvas component for this platform, so a different platform, architecture, or Linux libc needs a matching build. Starting from data and code Data and code are the core of reproducibility; the image is the result of one run. Under New , choose one of two starting points: Starting point Must provide What happens next --- --- --- Start from data (recommended) Data file, plotting request The AI inspects the data, writes code, freezes the inputs, actually runs it, and creates the first figure. Existing data and code Data file, Python code, request Saves the existing code and a data snapshot, runs once to establish a baseline; an existing image can be used for comparison. After you click Start plotting , check the run in the session on the left; when it finishes, refresh and select the figure. Later, keep typing changes on the Figure page; you do not need to reimport every raw data file. text Read data/trend.csv, use time as the x-axis and response as the y-axis. Draw a blue line chart with units on the axes. Do not fabricate data. Freeze this step's data and code and actually run it; for later changes, generate a candidate first and wait for my confirmation. File selection is a workspace file reference, not a browser upload entry point. With only an image, exact data cannot be restored. A supplied source image is marked "user-provided, not yet verified" and linked to the saved code and inputs; no past successful run is fabricated. The result of an actual run is kept as a separate version. What is saved at each step Record How it is saved --- --- Data Each code version has its own input byte snapshot, original relative path, SHA-256, and length. Child versions copy the parent's frozen data by default and do not re-read mutable workspace files. Code and parameters Full source file, entry point, parameters, and parent relationship; old versions are not overwritten. Run environment Python/Matplotlib versions, implementation, interpreter name, platform/architecture, and a list of installed Python package versions. Runs and artifacts Each run uses a new ID and records state, exit code, length-limited logs, and PNG, CSV, TSV, JSON, and TXT outputs; every file has a path, SHA-256, and byte count. Environment rebuild files A successful run automatically saves _environment/requirements.txt (exact versions), environment.json , and REBUILD.md . History Code, data, runs, source images, and candidates are all kept; Version history lets you view earlier figures. Accepting only changes the current figure pointer. When you modify code without changing data, the frozen inputs are inherited by default. To use updated data, tick Re-read workspace data in advanced settings to form a new version. If data cleaning, filtering, or transformation should feed the next step, you must first save the result file and include it in the next version's input snapshot; the plugin does not automatically capture the whole workspace or arbitrary variables in Python memory. Rerunning a specific version uses the code, parameters, and data bytes saved with it; rewriting or deleting the old source file should not change the saved snapshot. The environment listing helps you check dependencies, but it is not a portable container, a package binary archive, or a complete lockfile, and it does not guarantee identical image digests across platforms. Saving analysis artifacts, pagination, and recovery The script writes cleaned data and statistical results to SCIENTIFIC_FIGURES_OUTPUT_DIR , where they are saved alongside the figure, for example cleaned.csv , summary.json , and rules.txt . CSV/TSV/TXT must be valid UTF-8 and JSON must be parseable; an error fails explicitly rather than treating a bad file as a successful result. The PNG limit remains 16 files, 20 MiB each, 64 MiB total; analysis files have a separate limit of 32 files, 8 MiB each, 32 MiB total. To use a saved file in the next step, combine the workspace-relative .scientific-figures/ with the output.path returned by the run and put it into the new code version's inputPaths . That step copies and freezes the input again, so you do not have to manually save the staging file elsewhere in the workspace. Only PNGs can be published as figures ; data files can still be selected to view their saved path and summary. Code and runs shows 20 summary entries per page by default; click More code versions / More runs to load more. Full contents and verification files are fetched only when you read a selected record. A corrupted entry shows a local error and should not block other pages or break the record entry point. Trusted results from a terminated process are saved first, then artifacts are collected and submitted; staging is cleaned up only after submission succeeds. Among runs that have not finished or were interrupted , only entries with a trusted process result offer Complete interrupted record : this reuses the original result to finish the submission without rerunning Python. Entries with no result, an unconfirmed stopped process, or a leftover lock need inspection; the plugin will not guess success, steal the lock, or retry automatically. Rebuilding the environment The _environment directory of each successful run stores: the exact package version list, Python/platform/architecture information, and instructions for creating a virtual environment and installing dependencies. Match the recorded Python implementation, version, platform, and architecture first, then follow REBUILD.md in a separate virtual environment. The plugin only generates files and does not install packages automatically. The pinned-version file is not a hashed package lock and does not include binaries, drivers, system libraries, original index URLs, or editable source. Packages may be unavailable during a rebuild, and byte-identical images are not guaranteed across platforms. Old runs keep only the records that existed at the time and do not backfill historical environment files. Modifying, comparing, and accepting Keep describing changes in text, for example "keep the data, change the line to blue, shorten the title." The AI should save a new code version, actually run it, and publish the output as a candidate figure. - Current figure / After change : inspect the current version against the selected candidate. When several candidates exist, switch between them with the Candidate dropdown. - Request acceptance : sends an acceptance request into the session and waits for the host's formal approval. After confirming the object, click Allow in the approval, and only then does the current figure update. - Keep current figure : rejects the selected candidate and keeps using the current figure. Generating, publishing a candidate, and formally accepting are three separate steps. An AI reply of "done" does not mean it has been accepted; go by the actual operation result. After acceptance, the source image and the historical code and runs are still kept. When a figure changes, old candidates may lose their baseline and need to be regenerated. Viewing code and runs Open Code and runs when you need to verify the process; ordinary plotting does not require reading this first. 1. Select a version and click Load version to view the Python source. 2. After editing, click Save and freeze code to get a new child version; the old code is not overwritten. 3. Click Run frozen Python to see run status, exit code, and output. Expand parameters, input paths, source comparison, environment, and logs as needed. 4. A successful output can be published as a new figure or as a candidate for an existing figure; before publishing a candidate you need to read and select the current baseline. You can also expand All versions and sources to go from a specific figure to its linked code and run records. Case: modify a line chart and formally accept it This is a real application acceptance case from 2026-11-05, kept in the 0.4.0-mvp.10 page ; the data uses demo values and does not represent a research conclusion. It verified "chat request → freeze code → actual Python → candidate figure → formal approval → restart recovery." 1. Prepare data and the request The existing line chart has an x-axis of [1, 2, 3] and a y-axis of [1, 3, 8] . Provide the existing Python file in the panel and ask it to save a new child version with the y-axis changed to [2, 4, 7] , actually run it, publish a candidate, and not accept yet. text Based on the current line chart's Python code, keep the x-axis, change y to [2, 4, 7], save it as a new child version, and actually run it. Publish it as a candidate figure first; do not accept automatically. 2. Verify the actual output Item Measured result --- --- New code version chat-mvp-v5-20261105 , parent relationship preserved Run chat-mvp-run-v5-20261105 Run result completed , exit code 0 Environment Python 3.14.7 , Matplotlib 3.11.2 Output PNG, 960 × 720, 31,384 bytes Candidate r-ee889dbf7bff5aa71d3732541fa9d5a6 The chat auto-attached image was verified for real in 0.4.0-mvp.6 : after re-reading that run, the image decodes and displays normally. The screenshot comes from the actual chat attachment and was not redrawn. 3. Confirm acceptance and check after restart Click Request acceptance in the panel, and the session triggers the host's formal approval. After approval, the document revision becomes 7 and the current figure points to that candidate; the original figure is still kept. Then quit and restart SciForge: the chat box, file entry points, and accepted figure all recover, and the image still loads normally. FAQ Symptom Resolution --- --- AI finished but the panel still shows the old figure Click Refresh and check the figure and candidate selection. Sending fails Confirm that a working DSH session and model connection are available; keep your input and retry once the session recovers. Python or Matplotlib unavailable Check the error in Code and runs , configure the right interpreter and dependencies, then retry with a new run. Image auto-attachment shows File not found Update to a compatible version that includes the 0.4.0-mvp.6 fix, and ask the AI to re-read that run. Error paths already saved in old messages are not rewritten automatically. Cannot accept a candidate Check whether formal approval completed and whether the current document/baseline changed; do not hand-edit approval fields. Run failed but you still want to publish an image Fix it and run successfully first; a failed run cannot be published as a formal candidate. Current scope and boundaries - Implemented: Python + Matplotlib, saving PNG and CSV/TSV/JSON/TXT artifacts, code snapshots, dependency pin files, paginated history, interrupted-submission recovery, figure linking, and formal acceptance. R keeps the executor boundary, but execution is not implemented. - Inputs are workspace files. After a successful plot you must refresh manually; local dependencies and the model service are yours to configure. - On-image boxing, arrows, circling, and pin annotations are no longer provided. The old standalone Visual Review has also been retired. - Records are saved in .scientific-figures/ in the current workspace. They do not depend on Artifact Versions or Evidence DAG, and do not automatically register versions or evidence with them. Organize linked records separately when needed. - The first session limits the writable scope of the workspace; switching directories does not widen permissions. Running is refused in a read-only environment, when isolation is unavailable, or when the workspace is in the system temporary directory. - Local Python has write isolation, but that is not the same as prohibiting global reads or network access. Model requests are also subject to the data policy of the model service you use, so do not claim "data never leaves the machine." Only execute trusted code. - This case covers a representative local path and does not promise pixel-identical reproduction on every platform, Runtime, or environment. Related pages - Extension Center: installation sources, permissions, and enabling/disabling. - Runtime and models: prepare a working session. - Workspaces and sessions: confirm the file and task context. - Feature status and limitations: verified scope and release status.

en.title: SiYuan Notes
en.description: Connect your own SiYuan service to the workbench and archive traceable Markdown summaries after tasks finish.
en.body: SiYuan Notes SiYuan Notes connects a user-provided remote SiYuan service to the workbench as a full-page editor for reading, editing, and archiving research records. It is used in the organization stage after task execution, and you can also consult notes during a task. SciForge does not bundle the kernel or run or manage that service for you. How to open it - Entry: SiYuan Notes in the left sidebar opens the editor to the right of the session by default. From the page header you can move it to the left, bottom, or main area and resize it. Position and size are saved on this machine. - Target: the SiYuan service you run or subscribe to, along with its notebooks and documents. - Prerequisite: an accessible HTTP/HTTPS SiYuan address. If the service requires authentication, enter an API token in the page's settings, or use the SIYUAN_API_TOKEN environment variable. SciForge does not start or distribute the SiYuan kernel with the app. What you can do What you want to do How to do it Output --- --- --- Connect your own SiYuan Enter the service address in Settings on the page and save it; leave it blank to use the installation default An editor session that persists across restarts Edit and browse notes Use the SiYuan interface directly in the full-page editor Document changes in SiYuan Search and read existing notes Ask the Agent to search by path fragment, then read by document ID or path The note location and Markdown body; long notes are marked as truncated Archive task summaries automatically For a top-level Agent turn that finishes successfully and produces a final reply, SciForge writes an entry to a notebook automatically A Markdown document in SciForge 工作总结 , containing the request, final reply, time, and turn identifier Have the Agent write to a specific document Ask the Agent to save results to SiYuan and provide the title, notebook, and path The target document in SiYuan Typical workflow 1. First confirm in the SiYuan service that the target notebook exists and is writable. If authentication is required, prepare an API token and save it in the page's settings or set it in the launch environment. 2. Open SiYuan Notes from the left sidebar and enter the service address in Settings. If the page reports an error, retry or open Settings to correct it. 3. Read or edit in the editor. Do not place sensitive content that should not leave the local machine into a remote service. 4. After an Agent task completes normally, check whether a corresponding record appears under SciForge 工作总结 . If the service is temporarily unreachable, records queue and retry. Inputs, outputs, and permissions - Reads: the SiYuan service address, notebook list, and document content. The API token saved in the page's settings is used first; otherwise the environment variable is used. - Writes: documents in SiYuan. Automatic archiving writes to a fixed notebook, while Agent writes follow the requested title, notebook, and path. - Approval or external effects: archiving is an automatic external write after a successful task and does not prompt each time. Note content is sent to the configured SiYuan service, and the API token is used to authenticate to that service; confirm the service address and access scope before use. - What it does not do: start or bundle the SiYuan kernel, provide a local private mode, save to another location when the service is unreachable, and a token entered on the page is kept in the app's encrypted storage, not in the page's local configuration. Known limitations - Server mode only: you must provide an accessible SiYuan service, and the address must be HTTP/HTTPS. - The Content Space Provider currently declares notebook discovery only. You cannot upload or download files or perform native document operations through Content Space. - Automatic archiving covers only successful top-level Agent turns. Intermediate progress, failures, cancellations, and continuous sub-turns are not archived, and it does not produce a second AI summary or claim that the task is verified. - Archiving writes to the fixed notebook SciForge 工作总结 and the /SciForge path; the notebook is created if it does not exist. Retries of the same turn use a durable receipt to avoid duplicates. - SciForge does not ship the SiYuan kernel; using it on this machine also means deploying the service yourself. - When the service is unreachable or a write result is uncertain, pending records are kept locally and retried on the next task or at startup. Unconfirmed writes are not repeated blindly. Related pages - Content Space: how SiYuan connects as a Provider and its capability boundaries. - Collaboration: collaborative delivery and post-task local archiving are two different paths. - Permissions and security: external service addresses, tokens, and data boundaries. - Feature status and limitations: the capability scope of the first version. Implementation basis: @sciforge/domain-siyuan-content-space-provider v0.3.1.

en.title: Terminal
en.description: Run commands directly in the workspace, verify the results, and keep key output in the session.
en.body: Terminal Terminal puts the command-line environment for the current workspace in the bottom panel. It is suited to running scripts, checking logs, and confirming the status of long-running tasks. You type commands in the panel yourself; when the Agent runs commands in a session, it follows the Runtime's approval and sandbox policies. The permission settings for the two apply separately. How to open it - Entry: Terminal in the right toolbar (expand More tools if it is not shown), or Terminal in the bottom panel. - Target: the current workspace. The terminal process uses the workspace root as its initial working directory. - Prerequisite: a workspace is open, and the local or remote Workspace Host can start a system shell. - Tabs: a workspace can have multiple tabs (up to 8), with support for renaming, closing other tabs, closing all tabs, and restarting the process. What you can do What you want to do How to do it Output --- --- --- Run a one-off command Enter a command in a tab and press Enter Terminal output and the process exit status Watch a long-running task Keep the tab open and scroll through the ongoing output Task progress; closing the tab ends that terminal process Separate tasks Create and name separate tabs Command-line sessions isolated by tab Reproduce experiment steps Put the commands in a script, run it in the terminal, and record key output Commands you can run again, plus exit statuses Typical workflow 1. Confirm that the workspace shown at the top is the project this task should work on. 2. Open Terminal and run pwd and read-only commands first to confirm the directory, interpreter, and dependencies. 3. For commands that will write files, access the network, or install software, check the target paths, arguments, and recovery plan first. 4. Explain the purpose of the command in the session, and bring key output, exit statuses, or error messages back into the conversation. 5. Check the file state after the task. Copy terminal content you need to keep into notes or an artifact. Inputs, outputs, and permissions - Reads: commands can read files, environment variables, and network resources that the current user has permission to access. - Writes: commands can modify workspace files and may also write outside the workspace. The working directory is not a filesystem sandbox. - Approval or external effects: Terminal does not prompt for each command. Operations such as installing dependencies, accessing the network, and overwriting files take effect directly under the current user's permissions. - Agent execution: commands started by the Agent are governed by its Runtime's approval and sandbox settings. There is no promise that all commands skip approval, and no guarantee that every command triggers a prompt. - Output retention: commands and output stay with the tab in the current workspace and are not kept after the tab closes. Results from Agent-started commands return to the session context with the tool call. - What it does not do: it does not automatically write terminal content into the conversation record. Closing a tab ends the corresponding terminal process, but switching workspaces does not automatically end terminals that are already running. Known limitations - Terminal processes in remote workspaces run remotely, and output is read through incremental cursors. Remote controlled terminals are pipe-based and do not claim full pseudo-terminal (PTY) compatibility. - The tab limit is 8. Closing all tabs collapses the panel, and unsaved screen content is not restored. - Command availability depends on the shell, PATH, and dependencies on the local or remote host. SciForge does not install missing tools for you. - Terminal scrollback is limited. Write important output to files or logs, and use persistent scheduling or logging for long-running tasks. - Content in the manual terminal does not automatically enter the Agent context. To inform the Agent, paste the necessary excerpts into the session or have it run the commands itself. Related pages - Workbench tools: how files, Terminal, Browser, and Computer Use divide responsibilities. - Workspaces and sessions: workspace locations and session state. - Permissions and security: approvals, credentials, and the scope of command effects. - Remote resources and collaboration: terminals and data boundaries in remote workspaces. Implementation basis: @sciforge/domain-terminal v1.0.1.

en.title: Visual Review
en.description: Migration note for the old image-review entry point, and how to review figures now.
en.body: Visual Review In the current source baseline, the standalone visual-review plugin and the old static domain have both been removed. This page keeps its original URL so old links and historical records can still find it. The old toolbar entries and panel operations are no longer current steps. Do not treat the following from earlier versions as still available: box selection, arrows, circles, pins, review packages, split or overlay comparison, visual-spec recognition, and "accept and replace". The existence of old review data also does not mean the current implementation migrates or reads it automatically. Keep the original files and records, and check the recovery path separately. The current Scientific Figures is managed by the standalone Scientific Figures plugin. You describe the change in words as a Python + Matplotlib request, it runs the code to produce a candidate, and you accept it through the host's formal approval. It keeps its own immutable code, input, run, and image versions, and accepting updates the current-figure pointer. It has no on-image annotation interface, and it is not the old Visual Review's general source-image replacement service. To leave feedback on specific text or a registered task view, use the standalone Anchored Comments. Screenshots depend on host authorization and a capture service. Saving a comment does not mean the image was changed, a candidate was accepted, or an artifact version was registered. For cross-artifact source and delivery records, see Evidence & reproducibility.

en.title: Five-minute quickstart
en.description: Open a local project, analyze it read-only with Codex, and verify the file state before and after the task.
en.body: Five-minute quickstart Start by having the Agent examine a local project in read-only mode: open a workspace, confirm Codex's permissions, send a task, then compare the file state. When you are done, you should see a project overview and no changes to project files. This page reflects the current implementation as of 2026-11-06; older screenshots are kept as historical illustrations. For install-version differences, see versions and compatibility. 1. Prepare a project and a model Start SciForge, prepare a clean Git project or a copy of a project, and configure working model access and Codex. For the first run you can start from a local workspace without signing in to the collaboration cloud. In the first-run wizard or Settings → General , choose Model API or Coding Plan . Then go to Settings → AI assistant and check whether Codex is detected. Settings is at the bottom of the expanded left sidebar; account and cloud status are in the same area. Old interface: illustrates the two paths, Model API and Coding Plan. 2. Record the file state and set read-only permissions Run this in the project directory and save the output: bash git status --short If there are already modifications, record them clearly first; for a non-Git project, use a copy. Go to Settings → AI assistant → Codex and set File access range to Can only read files , keeping an appropriate tool approval policy. Wait for the setting to apply, finish any existing tasks, then reconnect or restart and start a new session. Old interface: “Can edit workspace” in the figure allows writes; change it to “Can only read files” before starting this tutorial. For detailed steps, see configure a read-only sandbox.
