Write the no-modification instruction into the prompt as well; if you see a request to widen permissions, stop and check, because this task needs no write access. 3. Open a local workspace and start a new session In the Workspace location menu, choose Local workspace, open the project directory, and check the path and the project name on the left. Start a new session, and confirm in the bottom input area that the execution runtime is Codex . The left side of the current workbench is for project, session, and collaboration navigation; the vertical toolbar on the far right opens tools such as files, and panels dock beside it. If there are many tools, open More tools . Old interface: shows a local project and a new session; the location of the current tool entry points is as described in the body text. 4. Send your first task Enter: Look at the current workspace, list only the top-level files and directories, and describe in one sentence what this project might be. Do not modify files or install dependencies. You do not need to add attachments for this task. To point at an existing file, use the file panel's reference action or type @ . Choosing files from outside your machine, dragging them in, or pasting images may import files into the workspace first, which changes the file baseline for the read-only check; save that for a later task. For the difference between the attachment tray and the labels on sent files, see workspaces and sessions. Old interface: shows the task text and the execution runtime. After sending, watch the tool calls, working directory, and execution results in the session. If the Runtime is not connected, check Settings → AI assistant and the model configuration first, then send again. Old interface: shows the execution state within the same session. 5. Verify the results and files The answer should list the top-level contents and give a grounded judgment about what the project is. Run again: bash git status --short Compare with the pre-task state and confirm that no project files were added, deleted, or modified. Git does not show ignored caches; when you need a strict check, also compare your copy's file list and content hashes. If you find changes, stop and investigate rather than restoring existing modifications outright. Old interface: the sample answer does not represent the results for your current project. Once you confirm that the workspace is correct, Codex responds normally, read-only permissions are applied, and the file state matches the pre-task state, you have completed your first task. Next, you can continue with: Continue the read-only analysis. Explain what the main directories are for, the likely entry files, and a recommended way to start or test the project. List anything that cannot be confirmed from the source separately. Do not modify files or install dependencies. Continue reading: Runtime and model access, working with the Agent.

en.title: Configure a read-only sandbox
en.description: Configure Codex's read-only execution scope, understand how Claude Plan mode differs, and compare Git status before and after a task.
en.body: Configure a read-only sandbox “Do not modify files” in a prompt is a task requirement; you also need to configure execution permissions. This page uses the Codex read-only sandbox as the getting-started path; the file-scope option of the same name in Claude Code corresponds to Plan mode , and the two isolate work differently. This article reflects the current implementation as of 2026-11-06; for install-version differences, see versions and compatibility. Where the setting lives 1. Expand the left sidebar and open Settings from the bottom. 2. Go to AI assistant . 3. In the AI assistant configuration cards at the top of the page, find Codex . 4. Find the File access range dropdown under that Runtime and select Can only read files . 5. Wait for the setting to apply, then reconnect or restart SciForge after finishing the current task; do not keep using a running task whose permissions are not yet confirmed. 6. Return to the workbench, start a new session, and confirm in the bottom-right of the input box that the execution runtime is codex . The Access shortcut at the top of the page jumps to the Computer Use configuration; the file access range is in each Runtime's own configuration section. Old interface: the value shown allows workspace changes; select “Can only read files” for read-only tasks. Runtime What “Can only read files” actually means Boundaries --- --- --- Codex Requests Codex's readOnly sandbox and disables command network access within that sandbox Suitable for the local file inspection in this tutorial; stop and check any request that widens permissions Claude Code Uses Claude Code's plan permission mode For analysis and planning; do not claim it provides the same filesystem sandbox isolation as Codex DSH Has no file access range option of the same name; the native shell is off by default and, once enabled for a DSH you installed, approved command by command This tutorial uses Codex; do not treat DSH's shell switch as a filesystem read-only sandbox MCP, remote commands, and Computer Use permissions must each be checked separately; for your first task, use only the tools needed to read the local project. Adding files from outside the workspace, dragging files in, or pasting images may import files into the workspace first. For a read-only check, reference existing files and record the baseline again once the import completes. Removing an attachment above the input box only cancels this send; it does not delete files that have already been imported. What read-only mode allows You can usually: - List directories and read text files - Search source and configuration - View Git status and diffs - Run checks that do not write to the workspace - Provide analyses, plans, and recommendations You should not allow: - Creating, overwriting, renaming, or deleting files - Installing dependencies that write to the project - Running commands that generate caches, logs, or build artifacts - Modifying the Git index, commits, or branches Whether a command is truly read-only depends on what it does, not what it is called. Some tests and interpreters generate caches automatically; if you hit a write failure in the read-only sandbox, change your checking approach rather than widening permissions just to finish the tutorial. Double verification In a Git project, run this before and after the task: bash git status --short Comparing Git status detects changes but does not replace execution isolation; it also does not list files ignored by .gitignore . When you need a strict check of every file, use a copy of the project and additionally compare the file list and content hashes before and after the task. If the output changes: 1. Stop any further tasks immediately. 2. Open the Changes panel from the vertical toolbar on the far right of the workbench or from More tools to check the files. 3. Do not automatically delete or restore existing modifications. 4. Determine whether the changes come from the task, from tool caches, or already existed before the task. Old interface: the Changes panel helps review diffs, but Git status still needs an independent check. When to switch to workspace write Switch to Can edit workspace only when a task explicitly needs to generate scripts, tables, figures, or documents and you have checked the plan and output paths. Write tasks should use a project copy or a clean branch, and you should review the changes when finished. Next: working with the Agent.

en.title: Runtime and model access
en.description: Configure model access, choose Codex, Claude Code, or DeepSeek Harness, and complete a connection check.
en.body: Runtime and model access Configure the model service first, then choose the AI assistant that executes tasks. The former determines where model requests go; the latter plans work and calls tools. This page reflects the current implementation as of 2026-11-06; for install-version and feature differences, see versions and compatibility. Setting Entry point What to confirm --- --- --- Model access First-run wizard or Settings → General The Model API base URL, key, and model, or official sign-in for Coding Plan AI assistant Settings → AI assistant Installation, connection, and permissions for Codex, Claude Code, or DeepSeek Harness (DSH) Current session Execution settings in the bottom input area The Runtime, model, and available tiers for this run Settings is at the bottom of the expanded left sidebar. Local accounts and SciForge cloud sign-in are managed separately, see Identity & Access. Choose model access With Model API , enter the Base URL, API Key, and model name provided by your service provider; if you are unsure about the protocol, use automatic detection. An existing key only means the field is configured; whether the upstream accepts it must be confirmed with an actual request. Old interface: use it only to recognize the fields; enter your own service configuration. With Coding Plan , complete official sign-in or device-code authorization in the interface. The Coding Plan path currently supports Codex; Claude Code uses model access. If sign-in or connection fails, fix the current access path according to the prompt, then retry. Choose and connect a Runtime In Settings → AI assistant , choose the execution runtime and check the detection result; if automatic detection fails, use Choose local app or enter the absolute path to the executable, then detect again. - Codex : uses the installed Codex app-server; check the model and permissions before starting a task. - Claude Code : configure model access and check its permission mode. - DSH : connects through a local ACP program; the model and reasoning tier take effect in the session after connecting. Check the program you specified, the system path, and common install locations first, and only try the component bundled with the app when none of them work. DSH's Shell command execution is off by default; enable it only for a DSH you installed yourself, and each run still requires approval. Do not switch to full permissions just to make an error go away. Old interface: shows execution runtime configuration, tool confirmations, and file scope. Codex and Claude Code can edit the workspace by default. For your first analysis, adjust permissions according to configure a read-only sandbox first. After switching execution runtimes, re-check the connection, sign-in, and permissions; existing sessions' mappings and configuration do not migrate automatically. When you need to operate desktop applications, also check Computer Use 's Runtime support, backend, and system permissions. Old interface: illustrates the configuration items that must be checked separately. Run a minimal connection check Start a new session, confirm that the expected Runtime is selected in the input area, and send: Reply only with “connected”. Do not read or modify files, and do not call external services. After you receive a response, continue to the five-minute quickstart. If the selected Runtime is unavailable, fix it according to the error or switch deliberately; the app will not automatically pick another Runtime for you. Troubleshoot DSH timeouts DSH distinguishes between a timeout on a single connection request and a task that makes no progress for a long time: Case Meaning and handling --- --- Initialization, create, or resume session requests time out The default single wait is 15 seconds. Check the local program, the connection, and any explicit error; extending the wait will not solve long-running tasks A task produces no session updates for a long time By default, the turn stops after 10 minutes of continuous silence; long tasks that keep receiving updates for the current session can exceed 10 minutes. Review the existing results before deciding whether to continue the same session For technical troubleshooting: the former's configuration name is requestTimeoutMs ; the latter, although named promptTimeoutMs , means the idle limit and has the error code runtime_prompt_idle_timeout . After a timeout, the original session identifier can be recovered, but you should still check existing files and external actions before continuing the task.

en.title: SciForge User Manual
en.description: From opening a project and handing the AI a task to checking results, saving records, and collaborating with your team.
en.body: SciForge User Manual In SciForge, you can open a project, let the AI read materials, modify files, run analyses, and create figures, then check the results and request changes. The files, conversations, and run records from a task remain available for review and for later collaboration. If this is your first time, start with the five-minute quickstart. If you already have a specific question, use the outline below to find the right page; there is no need to read the whole manual from beginning to end. The manual has six parts Part When to read it What it covers --- --- --- Getting started The first time you open SciForge Connect a model, choose an execution runtime, open a project, and complete a simple task; set read-only access or allow file changes. Workbench guides You want to know where a button is or how to hand files to the AI Workspaces and sessions, adding attachments, file preview, panel layout, Terminal and Browser Preview, as well as how to describe a task and check results. Features & Extensions You need to complete a particular kind of research work Scientific file preview, plotting and comments, versions and research records, team collaboration, notes, scheduled tasks, and extensions. Case tutorials You want to see how a complete task is done From input data through running an analysis, revising results, and delivering them; includes scientific plotting, multi-person RNA-seq collaboration, and virtual cell cases. Settings & security You need to adjust file access, tool permissions, or connected services File and network access, action confirmations, and the conditions for using remote resources and team collaboration. Reference & troubleshooting You hit an error or a version mismatch, or need to look up installation requirements Troubleshooting, versions and compatibility, feature limits, and extension licenses. Find a page by goal - Have the AI read a project first : five-minute quickstart. - Hand files to the AI and continue an earlier conversation : workspaces and sessions. - Open a sequence, molecular structure, or omics file : Life Science Preview. - Plot from data, then refine step by step : Scientific Figures. - See which files changed and save intermediate results : Evidence & Reproducibility. - Invite members, assign tasks, and review deliverables : team collaboration. - Install extensions or connect external tools : extensions and marketplace. - The interface does not match the tutorial : versions and compatibility. A few names to start with A workspace is the project directory you open. Which files the AI works on and where the Terminal runs both depend on it. A session is a conversation centered on a specific task. One project can have many sessions; keeping different goals in separate sessions makes them easier to pick up later. The Runtime (execution runtime) is the program that actually handles tasks. You can choose Codex, Claude Code, or DSH, then connect models and tools according to the instructions for each, see Runtime and model access. Research records hold a task's intermediate results and the basis for them. Once you have completed your first task, look into checkpoints, the Evidence DAG, and research dossiers as needed. This manual reflects the client update of 2026-11-06. Some case studies use earlier interfaces and keep their original version notes; see versions and compatibility for the specifics.

en.title: Documentation maintenance checklist
en.description: Maintain one user manual against the latest client, and check versions, links, and the public boundary.
en.body: Documentation maintenance checklist User tutorials are maintained only in sciforge-docs-v2 . The client repository keeps the site entry points, install and development notes, and internal supplements; it no longer duplicates the full tutorials. 1. Pin this round's version Record the date and commit of the latest client mainline first, then verify the interfaces, settings, package versions, and operations the change touches. Update Version and compatibility and the repository README. Record the public source commit separately; do not wait for it to update before writing the manual. Read the current implementation, not just the old README, test names, or planning documents. If a behavior exists only as a test expectation and is not wired into any actual call, list it as an item to verify; do not write it up as an operating step. 2. Update content and navigation - Write "where to open it, how to operate it, what you get" first, then the limits that affect the operation. - Use the actual names shown in the interface. Do not repeat the mainline commit, permission terms, and verification notes on every page; link to the version page instead. - When a feature moves, adjust the overview, sidebar, and related links. Keep a short migration note at the old URL and take it out of the current feature navigation. - English site: update the same-path pages under i18n/en/docusaurus-plugin-content-docs/current/ . When you add or remove a page or rename a sidebar category, also update i18n/en/docusaurus-plugin-content-docs/current.json . - Do not claim "all plugins are available" from a directory count. Describe built-in modules, standalone plugins, Skills, and MCP separately. - Keep the original date and version on screenshots and cases. Do not relabel them as a new-version demo unless re-recorded; add one sentence to outdated screens. 3. Check the public boundary The public site may describe user operations of the latest client. Internal deployment, database migration, VPN/SSH management, server-side adaptation, real account configuration, and private acceptance material stay in internal documents. General usage such as client sign-in, device connection, and team projects can be public. For new images, first check for visible accounts, paths, tokens, and rights to the material. Keep already-reviewed images; do not bulk-restore old media from the private repository. Keep plugin licenses, original-author attribution, and third-party notices as they are; documentation updates do not change licenses or repository visibility. 4. Keep entry points consistent The user-manual links on the public and private client home pages both point to https://agi4sci.github.io/sciforge-docs-v2/ . Old manual pages inside the repository keep a link to the matching site page. Internal supplements do not go into the public export. Later source exports must keep the licenses, replacement assets, security test fixtures, and these entry points that the public repository has already reviewed; do not overwrite the public repository with the private repository's directories. 5. Build and check bash npm ci npm run typecheck npm run build The build generates the search index and checks internal links. Also check whether retired features still appear on the home page, sidebar, search suggestions, and video chapter descriptions. A successful build only shows the docs can be built; the content still needs a page-by-page review. If the video is not re-recorded, keep the original file and chapter order, and note the applicable version on the guide page. When chapter data is involved, also run node scripts/check-tour.cjs . 6. Publish and spot-check Review through a PR, and wait for the GitHub Pages deployment to succeed after merging. Spot-check the home page, the version page, the feature overview, and this round's key pages online, and confirm the new content and page links work. The PR should state the basis for the update, the main pages, the check results, and any screenshots that need to be retaken later. If something goes wrong, roll back with a new revert PR; do not deploy an earlier site configuration.

en.title: Remote resources and collaboration
en.description: Distinguish remote workspace sessions from SciForge Cloud collaboration, and understand the data and permission boundaries of each.
en.body: Remote resources and collaboration Remote workspaces address "where compute and data live"; Cloud collaboration addresses "who works together around a Project and Task." The two can be combined or used independently. Remote workspaces A remote workspace brings a SciForge Workspace Host session running on another machine into the local workbench: files, terminals, Git, and Agent requests act on the remote directory, while the interface stays on your machine. - Entry point: the Workspace location selector at the top of the workbench, which switches between Local workspace and attached remote sessions; the selector also shows each remote session's lifecycle (Persistent server / Connection session), connection status (Remote, Reconnecting, Offline, Limited, Connection error), and network exit. - When a session disconnects or errors, use Reconnect on the target session in the selector. - The open-source client does not include a connection management panel for registering SSH targets, VPN environments, and workspace authorization; remote sessions appear in the selector only after the deployer provides and attaches them. Remote files, terminals, and Agent commands actually act on the remote directory. Do not mistake "displayed in a local window" for "the data has been copied to your machine." After connecting, check the remote path and file reads first, then test the terminal and the tools you need. If one tool reports that it is unavailable, do not conclude that the entire remote workspace is unusable; for the specific scope, see Version and compatibility. Cloud collaboration Use Cloud collaboration when you need to continue a personal Session on your phone, or when a team needs to assign and accept Tasks around a Project. It requires the Cloud service address, account, and collaboration service configuration provided by your administrator. For team procedures, see Collaboration guide; for a real submission, revision, and downstream handoff, see Pasilla three-person collaboration case. Check the sign-in and device prerequisites for team collaboration in that guide; setting up a personal Session on your phone is a separate path. Figure 2: Cloud connection status and the local workspace are independent of each other. Unified sign-in has three distinct states: State Purpose --- --- Local account Marks the current user and ownership on this machine Cloud sign-in Confirms your cloud identity Device connection Click Connect this device to authorize the current desktop installation to access Cloud capabilities A local account is not cloud authentication; a connected workspace also does not mean you have joined a collaboration Project. In collaboration, Shared files is for viewing resources provided by the content service; there is currently no direct upload entry point. Task delivery follows the Task submission and acceptance process; do not treat the Shared files entry as a general-purpose cloud drive upload. Figure 3: Team collaboration revolves around Projects, Tasks, owners, and acceptance results. Data and credential boundaries - SSH keys, VPN credentials, and MFA are managed by the user or by system security infrastructure. - Cloud, collaboration services, and Content Space may send data to external services. - Before uploading production data, confirm the destination, scope, retention policy, and team permissions. - Remote commands and collaborative tasks should still record inputs, outputs, return codes, and approvals. - After a network interruption, confirm the state of the remote process before deciding whether to retry, to avoid submitting compute twice. Case: Virtual cell perturbation prediction benchmark.

en.title: Permissions and security
en.description: Choose read-only, workspace write, approval, and Computer Use permissions according to the impact of the task.
en.body: Permissions and security First choose the file access range for the task, then check the terminal, plugin, remote service, and computer-use permissions you will use. Confirm the workspace and output locations before running, and verify the destination before submitting or uploading. File access range Range Suitable tasks Main risks --- --- --- Can only read files Project understanding, code review, data inventory, and planning Codex uses a read-only sandbox; Claude uses Plan mode, and the two are not equivalent Can edit workspace Modifying code and generating analyses, figures, and reports Overwriting existing files, writing to the wrong directory, and mixing in unrelated changes Can access all files Controlled tasks that explicitly require cross-directory reads or writes Removes read-only or workspace scope limits and runs tools automatically, potentially affecting data and configuration outside the workspace For a first task, an unfamiliar repository, or an unreviewed Skill, start with the Codex read-only configuration. Both Codex and Claude allow workspace writes in their initial configuration, so you must change this deliberately; MCP, remote execution, and Computer Use each require separate permission checks. For details, see Configuring a read-only sandbox. Approval policy An approval request should state at least: - What operation will be performed - The target files, directories, hosts, or external services - Whether it will write, upload, send, or delete - Whether it can be retried safely after a failure - How to check the result and recover The absence of an approval dialog does not mean an operation is read-only. Manual terminals run with the current system user's permissions; plugins must also be installed, enabled, and granted permissions for the relevant version separately. Credentials - Do not put API keys, tokens, or passwords in prompts, Git repositories, or screenshots. - MCP, the Model API, and collaboration services should each use the minimum credential scope they need. - Do not treat a provider key as a Runtime login credential. - Before exporting logs, traces, or a research dossier, check for Authorization headers, server addresses, real paths, and sample privacy. Computer Use Computer Use may operate other desktop apps, so it is constrained at the same time by SciForge settings, backend status, and macOS Screen Recording/Accessibility permissions. Figure 1: Before enabling it, check the allowed Runtime, Backend, and operating-system permissions together. The following actions should be confirmed by the user at the moment they are performed: account sign-in or authorization, sending messages, uploading data, purchasing or paying, deleting external content, and submitting formal evaluation results. When Scientific Figures accepts a candidate figure, it requires a formal tool call in the session and host confirmation; "Request acceptance" in the panel only initiates the request. Deleting anchored comments and submitting feedback also have their own confirmation steps; see the corresponding feature pages for details. Research data security - Use public or redistributable data for tutorials. - Do not overwrite raw data by default; write derived results to a separate directory. - Whether data in a remote workspace may be downloaded is determined by the project policy. - External models, MCP, and web uploads change the data boundary and must be evaluated separately. - Screenshots should hide real account names, keys, patient information, and server details. Pre-task checklist - [ ] The workspace or project copy is correct - [ ] A Git baseline has been recorded - [ ] The Runtime and file access range match the task - [ ] Output directories and overwrite policy are clear - [ ] Boundaries for network, installation, sign-in, and upload are clear - [ ] Acceptance and recovery methods are clear

en.title: Feature status and limitations
en.description: Distinguish source verification, historical real-world acceptance, and public release status by the latest implementation.
en.body: Feature status and limitations This round verifies the implementation against 2026-11-06 · mainline 3f6b0c3 . The table below does not automatically promote earlier real-world cases to cross-platform acceptance for the latest version; installer and Marketplace release status must be checked separately. Version and compatibility explains how these baselines relate. Capability Status this round Current scope and limitations --- --- --- Workspace, session, and workbench layout Implementation verified The vertical toolbar on the right, the account area in the sidebar, and the panel layout follow the latest implementation; historical screenshots may use an older layout. Codex / Claude Code Current entry points and configuration verified Choose the Runtime explicitly; models, sign-in, file permissions, and tool permissions are configured separately, and different executors are not treated as a silent fallback. DSH Runtime Implementation verified Long tasks use an idle timeout, and ongoing progress in the same session can renew it; the connection check and action confirmation each have their own time limit. Attachments and file references after sending Implementation verified Selecting, dragging, or pasting a file puts it in the attachment tray; the file reference is retained after sending. A file reference does not mean every Runtime receives embedded binary data. Text, code, and other file previews Implementation verified Whether you can edit depends on the format, whether the content was truncated, and whether a write-back channel exists; the interface should show why a file is read-only. Local accounts, cloud devices, and usage Implementation verified Deleting a local account does not delete the cloud account or your files; cloud identity and model provider identity are managed separately. Collaboration Requires an available service, roles, and task authorization Entry points for boards, members, requirements, shared files, and project information; shared files come from task delivery, and direct upload is not currently offered. The historical Pasilla case keeps its original verification scope. Biology Workbench preview Bundled implementation verified Large files may show only a summary; after changing a molecule selection, reopen it to recheck. Scientific Figures Current implementation MVP.11; historical local acceptance MVP.10 Frozen data and code, real Python, analysis artifacts, pagination, recovery, and environment rebuild files; the MVP.10 macOS arm64 + DSH evidence is retained, and it is not used to claim an all-platform or public Marketplace release for MVP.11. R is not implemented. Anchored Comments Standalone plugin Capture and external feedback require the corresponding host capabilities; deleting and submitting feedback have explicit approvals. Change Inspector Standalone read-only plugin Lets the Agent list the file differences in this session, paginated when too long; the old Changes panel has been removed. Artifact versions, checkpoints, Evidence / Project DAG, dossiers Available conditionally; verify per package The bundled features can be used as described on each page; the optional Evidence / Project DAG plugins cannot yet replace the bundled features. Scheduled tasks and Create Loop Requires the app to be running and an execution environment Task triggering, approvals, and restart boundaries follow each page; this is not a guarantee of a system-level unattended service. Plugin Marketplace, Skills, MCP Available conditionally A failed Marketplace read, no installable packages, and an empty search are handled separately; source code, signed packages, and a public Marketplace listing are separate matters. Dataset API / Scientific Compute / old Visual Review No longer part of the current standalone feature set Old links keep a migration note; the old operation entry points are no longer offered. Remote SSH management Internal supplement The public site does not provide VPN, SSH target registration, or server-side operating steps. Virtual cell models, Slurm/PBS/Kubernetes scheduling Not promised as bundled capabilities You can connect them in an authorized external environment; a tutorial is not a delivery of a model or a scheduling service. How to read verification status Source and contract verification shows that an implementation path exists; automated tests show that the scenarios they cover pass; real operation or installer acceptance must state the version, platform, and date. None of the three replaces the others. A passing documentation build this round also does not mean every client feature has been re-verified. When you file an issue, include the client and plugin versions, your system, the entry point, reproduction steps, and redacted screenshots. If a historical case disagrees with the latest interface, check the version page first, then report the specific difference in the body text.

en.title: Plugin licenses
en.description: Licenses, historical directory scope, and distribution notes for the seven current standalone plugins.
en.body: Plugin licenses The table below lists the versions and licenses of the 7 current plugin packages. See each feature page for installation requirements and Version and compatibility for how the versions relate. Plugin / source directory Source version Declared license npm private field --- --- --- --- Anchored Comments / plugins/anchored-comments 0.2.1 MIT true Change Inspector / plugins/change-inspector 0.1.2 MIT true Evidence DAG / plugins/evidence-dag 1.0.0 Apache-2.0 true Git Checkpoints / plugins/git-checkpoints 0.1.0 MIT true Project DAG / plugins/project-dag 1.0.0 Apache-2.0 Not set Research Checkpoints / plugins/research-checkpoints 0.1.0 MIT true Scientific Figures / plugins/scientific-plotting 0.4.0-mvp.11 MIT; the NOTICE and third-party licenses below are also retained true Source, installers, and npm publication - Source license : The entries above are each package's license declaration; using and redistributing the package still requires retaining the applicable LICENSE, copyright, and NOTICE. The repository root license cannot be used to override plugins or third-party components that carry their own license declarations. - Installer contents : Which code, native components, and license files an actual artifact contains must be checked against that version's package contents. A file existing in the source directory does not mean it is necessarily included in the build; this page does not certify any installer it has not inspected. - npm private: true : This field prevents ordinary npm publication. It does not mean the source is confidential, commercially proprietary, or barred from use under the existing license, and it does not mean the package cannot be distributed as a signed installer. Leaving the field unset also does not prove that the package has been published. - Release status : Version, license, installation authorization, and Marketplace availability are separate matters; rely on the specific release record and a trusted installation source. Retained notices for Scientific Figures The package declares MIT and must still retain its NOTICE : src/worker/ comes from the plotting worker originally released under Apache-2.0 (historical commit 02e7abb2 ), and moving or merging directories does not remove its Apache-2.0 terms. Redistributing these worker sources separately should also carry the original Apache-2.0 terms and applicable notices. The MIT declarations for the historical domain and adapter code are retained as well. The current build includes the JavaScript and the actually loaded platform native package for @napi-rs/canvas 0.1.100 , under dist/node_modules in the artifact. Third-party components in the package keep their own licenses; when distributing, check the license files inside the actual installer, the identity of the native package, and dist/native-runtime.json , rather than copying only the MIT row from this table. Changing platform, architecture, or Linux libc requires a matching build. Historical directories and scope Old plugins in the public repository carry their own LICENSE. When you update or migrate code, retain the corresponding license and attribution. Historical directory Historical license / current status --- --- plugins/biology-room Historical plugin MIT; the standalone directory is now retired, and the room functionality is provided by the bundled Biology Workbench 1.1.3 plugins/life-science-preview Historical plugin MIT; the standalone directory is now retired, and previews are provided by the same bundled Biology Workbench plugins/visual-review Historical plugin MIT; the standalone plugin and the old static domain have both been removed, see the migration note Old scientific-compute and dataset-api domains Now retired, see the migration pages for Scientific Compute and Dataset API; not counted among the seven plugins The licenses of the historical directories continue to apply to the code released at the time; deleting a directory, bundling a feature, or migrating a page does not constitute relicensing. The bundled Biology Workbench is part of the application source and should not simply inherit the old plugin's MIT declaration. When reusing historical code, go back to the LICENSE, NOTICE, and file headers of the corresponding version to confirm the applicable terms.

en.title: Troubleshooting
en.description: Diagnose SciForge problems across five layers: interface, Runtime, model access, permissions, and external services.
en.body: Troubleshooting First determine which layer the problem is in, so you do not change models, the Runtime, permissions, and workspace settings all at once. Five-layer quick diagnosis Layer Check first --- --- App interface Whether SciForge started correctly and the current workspace is the right one Runtime Whether Codex, Claude Code, or DSH is currently selected, whether the command can be found, and whether sign-in is valid Model access Whether the Model API or Coding Plan is fully configured Permissions and tools File access range, approvals, the Computer Use Backend, and system permissions External services Whether Cloud, MCP, Worker, or Provider is reachable; whether a remote workspace session is still attached Runtime shows as disconnected 1. Open Settings → AI assistant and confirm the current Runtime. 2. In your system terminal, check whether codex , claude , or dsh can be found. 3. If automatic detection fails, enter the absolute path to the executable. 4. After changing it, reconnect or start a new session. 5. Do not expect an automatic switch to another Runtime after a failure. Runtime is connected but the model does not respond - Confirm whether you are using a Model API or a Coding Plan. - A Model API requires a Base URL, API Key, and model name that match completely. - A Coding Plan requires a valid official sign-in state. - The current Coding Plan path supports Codex; if you select Claude Code, configure the Model API. - Do not put a Provider API key in the Runtime sign-in field. - Test with a minimal prompt that reads no files first, then investigate tools and the sandbox. A read-only task still changes files 1. Stop the task immediately. 2. Compare git status --short before and after the task. 3. Have the installed and authorized Change Inspector inspect the current session changes and compare them with the actual files. 4. Confirm the executor, whether settings were applied, and whether you approved expanded permissions; Claude Plan mode is not the same as the Codex read-only sandbox. 5. Check whether tests, interpreters, MCP, remote tools, or Computer Use wrote anything. Files ignored by Git need a separate check. 6. Do not automatically delete user changes that existed before the task. Scientific files are not understood - Check the extension, file version, and workspace reference. - Do not paste large files directly into a prompt. - Confirm in the file preview whether the format is supported; look for size limits or read errors. - When the current Provider does not support a binary format, it should explicitly degrade or stop rather than guess at the content. Evidence DAG or dossier is empty These panels do not generate evidence automatically from an empty session. First have the task explicitly record the research question, inputs, methods, claims, sources, artifacts, and limitations, then refresh the corresponding panel. The remote workspace is interrupted - In the workspace location picker, confirm the remote session state (remote, reconnecting, offline, or connection error). - Use Reconnect on a session that is offline or has errored; if reconnecting fails, switch back to a local workspace and continue local tasks. - Check whether the remote command is still running, and do not resubmit a long computation when the state is unknown. - After the connection is restored, check the logs, output files, and return codes. Include when filing an issue - SciForge version and operating system - The selected Runtime and how model access is configured - Workspace type: local or remote - Minimal reproduction steps and the time it occurred - Redacted logs or screenshots - Expected behavior and actual behavior Before submitting, remove API keys, Authorization headers, account names, server information, sample privacy data, and real sensitive paths.

en.title: Version and compatibility
en.description: Find the applicable versions for the client, plugins, and cases.
en.body: Version and compatibility This manual describes how to use the latest client. This round is updated against the mainline version 3f6b0c3 from 2026-11-06 . If you cannot find a button described in a tutorial, check your client and plugin versions first. Where to find version information Item Version this round Notes --- --- --- Client Mainline 3f6b0c3 The interface and feature basis for this round of tutorials. Public source 57ac3d0 observed this round, public sync 141 The development mainline and the public code may have different update times; rely on the commit you actually downloaded. Scientific Figures plugin 0.4.0-mvp.11 MVP.10 screenshots and run results in historical tutorials keep their original version. Installers and other plugins Check the download instructions, extension list, and release records Having source code or usage instructions does not mean the corresponding installer is listed in the Marketplace. Old screenshots and the new interface Some screenshots and videos in the tutorials come from earlier versions. When looking for entry points, follow the current description: - Commonly used tools have moved to the vertical toolbar on the right; when the window is not tall enough, some tools move into More tools . - When the left sidebar is narrowed, it usually keeps only icons; account and settings are at the bottom of the sidebar. Narrow windows may switch to an overlay. - After you select, drag, or paste a file, you can check it in the attachment tray, and after sending you can still open the file reference from the message. - To install plugins, open Extensions and go to the Market tab. - Collaboration projects are divided into “board, members, requirements, shared files, and project information”. For complete steps, see Workbench, Account, and Collaboration. Cases keep their own date, version, and system; an operation that has not been redone does not have its verified version changed. Feature migration Old feature How to use it now --- --- Biology Room, Life Science Preview standalone plugins Merged into Biology Workbench, so no separate installation is needed; they cover biology objects and scientific file previews respectively. Dataset API, Scientific Compute Retired. To obtain data or run computations, use the Agent tools, scripts, and environment you have configured. Old built-in Anchored Comments, Change Inspector Use the corresponding standalone plugins; see each tutorial for installation requirements. Old Scientific Plotting / Visual Review Use Scientific Figures for plotting; the old Visual Review is no longer offered as a standalone plugin. Plugin licenses lists each plugin's version, license, and installation requirements. Documentation and release notes This website is the unified user manual, and the documentation repository maintains the body text. Wiki pages in the client repository remain as entry points, and internal documentation separately holds deployment, remote management, and development records. This round updates the tutorials from the code and did not re-run every feature on every platform. Runs and screenshots that were actually completed are noted in the cases; see Feature status for current limitations. If you run into a problem, provide your system, the client and plugin versions, the steps you took, and redacted screenshots.

en.title: Working with the Agent
en.description: Write tasks as goals, scope, constraints, and acceptance criteria, and check tools and approvals during execution.
en.body: Working with the Agent State the goal, allowed scope, deliverables, and stop conditions clearly so that every step the Agent takes can be checked. This page reflects the current implementation as of 2026-11-06; for installed-version differences, see Version and compatibility. The four parts of an executable task Part Question to answer Example --- --- --- Goal What problem should ultimately be solved? Find the root cause of the failing test Scope Where may the Agent read and modify? Only the current package; do not change public APIs Constraints Which actions must not run automatically? Do not install dependencies or access the internet Acceptance How do you prove it is done? Relevant tests pass, with the root cause and changes explained Recommended template: text 目标：…… 范围：…… 约束：…… 交付物：…… 验收方式：…… 遇到以下情况请停止：…… Read first, plan next, write last For unfamiliar projects or research data, three rounds are recommended: 1. Read-only analysis : Have the Agent establish a baseline for the project, data, and risks. 2. Plan review : Check the files to be modified, output paths, dependencies, and verification method. 3. Execute and verify : Switch to the appropriate permissions, complete the writes, and review the diff. Legacy interface: shows the task text and execution status. Check input files Add material through Attach file in the input area, drag and drop, paste, or file references. Before sending, check the file names, paths, and types in the attachment tray and remove entries you do not need to send; after sending, open a preview from the file chips below the message. Workspace path references let the Agent read files on demand; they do not automatically embed the full text in the prompt. Importing external files writes to the workspace; read-only tasks should reference existing files. For details, see Workspaces and sessions. Watch the execution During execution, focus on: - The step the Agent is currently working on - The files it actually reads - Tool calls and their parameters - Commands, return codes, and output - Files written and their target paths - Approval requests waiting for your decision Before approving, check the operation's target, scope of impact, external destinations, and recovery method. To view files or diffs, open a panel from the far-right vertical toolbar; pages that support docking can be moved to the side or bottom and viewed alongside the session. In collaborative tasks, questions are answered by the designated member; action confirmations require a note and an explicit approve or reject. After submitting a decision, keep watching the execution results, and finally have a member review the delivery and the owner accept it. See Collaboration. Correct incomplete results Don't just say "be more detailed." Cite the specific gap: You listed the entry files but did not explain the call chain from startup to the main interface. Continue the read-only analysis and list the functions and source paths in call order; mark anything speculative separately. Split long tasks Break long tasks into phases that can be accepted independently, and state the inputs, outputs, and stop conditions for each. Research tasks in particular should stop when a data audit fails, rather than continuing to generate charts and reports that look complete. Next: Workbench tools.

en.title: Workbench tools
en.description: Open tools from the right-side vertical toolbar and understand docked pages, session panels, and execution permissions.
en.body: Workbench tools The current tool entry point is the workbench's far-right vertical toolbar , with panels expanding to its left. Entries appear according to installed extensions, the current session, and available capabilities; when space is tight, open More tools , or use Customize toolbar to adjust which supported entries appear and their order. This page reflects the current implementation as of 2026-11-06. What older text or images call the "top bar" is now on the right; for installed-version differences, see Version and compatibility. Tool Best for Key checks --- --- --- Files & Preview Browsing directories, previewing text, spreadsheets, images, or scientific objects, and referencing task inputs Workspace path, file version, and the difference between a reference and actually reading the contents Terminal Running commands and checking logs and long-running task status Working directory, parameters, return codes, and write and network impact Browser Viewing local previews or research material URL, sign-in state, downloads, and external submissions Computer Use Operating desktop apps on supported backends Runtime capability, backend, system permissions, and authorization for each action Change Inspector Having the Agent review this session's file changes Requires the plugin to be installed; check overall workspace state separately with git status --short Artifacts, Checkpoints & research panels Viewing phase results, evidence, and deliverables Actual installation state, input sources, versions, and unverified items An entry being present does not mean the backend is ready, nor that the Agent is authorized to perform external operations. The available scope of each extension is governed by its actual status and error messages. Docking and session panels Dockable extension pages can be moved to the left, right, bottom, or main area with the position control; multiple pages on the same edge switch via tabs. Moving a page organizes your workspace; it does not change project files or execution permissions. A session's right panel has its own layout: you can resize it, switch the bound content, split it where the panel supports it, and move forward and back through panel history. Clicking the toolbar acts on the currently focused panel; not all panels allow splitting. Confirm the current session and focused object before reviewing results. Check the actual impact of tools - Verify the workspace path, especially after switching between multiple sessions or projects. - For terminal commands, check the input, output paths, network targets, and return codes. - Browser downloads, account sign-ins, and form submissions can have external effects. - Actions in Computer Use such as sending, authorizing, deleting, and paying should be authorized individually. - A panel preview is not task acceptance; explain tool results in the session and flag failures or incomplete parts. Legacy interface: shows that the Runtime, Backend, and macOS permissions must each be satisfied; see this page for the current entry point. For file inputs, see Workspaces and sessions; for permissions, see Configuring a read-only sandbox and Permissions and security.

en.title: Workspaces and sessions
en.description: Organize projects and sessions in the sidebar, and check task inputs with the attachment tray and sent-file chips.
en.body: Workspaces and sessions A workspace determines where the Agent reads files, inspects Git, and runs commands; a session stores the messages, executions, and results around one goal. The same workspace can have multiple sessions. This page reflects the current implementation as of 2026-11-06; for differences between installed versions and the public source, see Version and compatibility. Get to know the current layout - Left sidebar : Organizes workspaces, sessions, and navigation contributed by extensions. Expand it to view collaborative projects, My Work, and the Inbox; local account, cloud status, usage summary, and Settings sit at the bottom. - Center session area : View tasks, tool calls, and answers, and enter tasks at the bottom. - Far-right vertical toolbar : Opens panels such as Files; when space is tight, find entries under "More tools." Which tools appear depends on what is installed and available. - Docked panels : Pages that support docking can be placed on the left, right, bottom, or in the main area; the session's right panel can also be split, resized, switched, and navigated forward and back where supported. The two layouts are not the same toggle. When the sidebar is collapsed, the full account summary and project tree are hidden; expand it first when you need those entries. Open a workspace 1. In the workspace location selector, choose a local workspace or a configured, available target. 2. Select the directory containing your paper, code, or data. 3. Verify the workspace path and the project name in the sidebar, then create a session. 4. Use a new session for a new goal; continue the existing session for the same goal. Legacy interface: illustrates the relationship between projects and sessions; for toolbar and account entry locations, use the current layout described on this page. Add files: choose, drag, paste, or reference Attach file in the input area opens the file picker; you can also drag supported files into the input area or paste files and images from the clipboard. Pasting ordinary text is still handled as text. PDFs, images, scientific data, and web documents are checked against type- and size-specific rules; unsupported files or failed imports show an error. Open the Files panel from the far-right toolbar to browse, preview, and reference workspace objects. You can also type @ to find workspace files; references containing spaces use the @"directory/filename" form. Before sending, the attachment tray above the input box lists the objects to send with their type, path, and known size. You can preview references that support preview or remove entries you do not need to send this time. After sending, the sent file chips below your message keep the file name and known size; click one to preview the corresponding workspace file. It is not a pending list you can keep editing. Input form Current handling Boundary to understand --- --- --- Files already in the workspace Keeps a workspace-relative path reference File contents are not fully embedded in the model prompt just because an attachment chip appears; the Agent calls tools to read them as needed Supported files selected or pasted from outside the workspace Imports them into the workspace's session attachment directory, then treats them as path references Importing writes to the workspace; removing a pending entry does not delete the imported file Supported model image attachment paths Handles images through the Runtime's attachment capability; the exact input depends on the Runtime, model, and image-processing configuration Unlike workspace path references, this may involve embedded images or image conversion; a file chip does not prove that the model read the original image directly The current workbench prefers to save images as workspace references when a workspace exists. Do not read "Attach file" as syncing an entire directory to the cloud or guaranteeing that the model has understood the file's contents. A read-only demo should reference existing files directly to avoid file changes caused by extra imports. Legacy interface: shows the purpose of directory browsing and preview; the current entry point is in the far-right vertical toolbar. Manage sessions and review changes Click a session to continue its goal, use search to find history, archive sessions you are not using for now, and restore them as needed. Save important results to the workspace or a research record before deleting. Do not mix unrelated research goals in one session. After modifying files, ask the Agent to use the Change Inspector to review this session's changes, then run git status --short to inspect the entire workspace. Closing a panel or switching sessions does not undo file modifications. Legacy interface: the old panel has been removed; this image is kept only as a diff-reading example. A clear session opening: Read the README, dependency configuration, and main entry points in the current workspace. First give the shortest path to run and test, without installing dependencies or modifying files; list anything you cannot confirm separately. Related pages: Working with the Agent, Workbench tools, Identity & Access.
